1.1: 1.1 Forasmuch as, etc. BEDE. Luke concerning all that Jesus did and taught, etc., down to they would arrange the narrative rather than weave the truth of history.
1.3: 1.3 All things. THE SAME. Not all that he had gained, but he believes suitable matters from all of them for confirming the faith of readers. For he deliberately passes over many things that others tell, so that a diverse grace might shine forth in the Gospel, and so that in each book the miracles of certain mysteries and deeds proper to it might stand out. Theophilus. Theophilus, lover of God, etc., down to he ought to know the order of the faith of the everlasting divinity and of his temporal dispensation.
1.5: 1.5 There was in the days of Herod, king of Judea. AMBROSE. The calf is the priestly victim. Therefore this Gospel is figured by the calf, in which it is begun by priests and completed in the calf, that is, in Christ, who is sacrificed for the life of the world. A certain priest. He has completed the order: he named the king and the region in which he lived, and he indicates the priest and his nation and his wife. Zacharias. Zacharias, mindful of the Lord: to whom the angel appears on the right of the altar, because the mystery is shown to him who is mindful of the Lord. Of the course of Abia. BEDE. Abia, Father the Lord, etc., down to as the Old Testament is declared by seven. Elizabeth. Elizabeth, fullness of my God, signifies Mary, who was full of God.
1.6: 1.6 And they were both. BEDE, AMBROSE. A full praise, which embraces lineage in his ancestors, character in uprightness, office in the priesthood, conduct in the commandments, and judgment in the justifications. Just before God. AMBROSE. For not everyone who is just before men is just before God; for men see one way, God another: men look at the face, God at the heart. And so it can happen that someone seems just to me by a studied goodness pleasing to the people, and yet is not just before God, if his justice is not formed from simplicity of mind but is feigned by flattery.
1.7: 1.7 And they had no son. BEDE. It was divinely arranged that John should be born of persons advanced in age and long deprived of the fruit of marriage, so that the unexpected birth of offspring might affect them more gratefully with the gift of God, and the astonishment at the miracle might prepare the others to hear the future prophecy. Hence it is afterwards added: All who heard laid it up in their heart, saying: What think you shall this child be?
1.8: 1.8 And it came to pass. Although by the precept of Moses, when one priest died, one was ordered to succeed, in the time of David it was established that those ministering by turns for eight days, from sabbath to sabbath, in the time of their turn, should each devote himself to purity and meanwhile not touch their house.
1.9: 1.9 By lot. BEDE. He was not chosen then by a new lot, when the incense was to be offered, etc., down to it is foretold while the former is promised as forerunner.
1.12: 1.12 And Zacharias seeing him was troubled, and fear fell upon him, etc. AMBROSE. We are accustomed to be troubled and estranged from our own feeling when we are struck by the encounter of a higher power. But as it is the weakness of man to be terrified, so it belongs to angelic kindness to console with a gentle look the one who is afraid; the demons, on the contrary, if they sense anyone terrified by their presence, shake them with greater horror.
1.13: 1.13 Your prayer is heard: and your wife Elizabeth shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name. It was heard more than you asked. You asked for the deliverance of the people, and a forerunner was given to you. AMBROSE. Many divine benefits are heaped together here. First, the fruit of prayer; then a barren woman's childbearing. Then the joy of many, and greatness of virtue; the prophecy of the Most High is also promised. Moreover, lest there be any doubt, the name of the one to come is designated. With so many things flowing beyond his wish, not undeservedly is his distrust punished with the penalty of silence.
1.14: 1.14 And you shall have joy, etc. BEDE. It is the sign of singular merit whenever a name is either given or changed for men by God, etc., down to because this one proclaims salvation to many, but that one gives it to all. AMBROSE. Joy and gladness. Parents are admonished to give thanks no less, etc., down to the mothers, because they are honored with the rewards of marriage.
1.15: 1.15 Wine and strong drink, etc. BEDE. It is a mark of great virtue before God to preach heavenly joys in the desert, etc., down to and already the spirit of grace was there.
1.16: 1.16 And he shall convert many of the children of Israel. THE SAME. Since John, bearing witness to Christ and baptizing in the faith of Christ, is said to have converted the children of Israel to God, it is plain that Christ is the Lord God of Israel.
1.17: 1.17 He shall go before. THE SAME. As Elijah is the herald of the judge, etc., down to that one is manifested with him in glory. In the spirit and power. AMBROSE. Spirit and power are well joined. For there is no power without spirit, nor spirit without power. Elijah had the power of abstinence and patience, and of turning the minds of peoples from unbelief to faith, and he had the spirit of prophesying. That he may turn, etc., BEDE. He turns the hearts of the fathers to the children, etc., down to almost the same words which the angel spoke of John, Malachi foretold of Elijah.
1.18: 1.18 Whereby, etc. THE SAME. If it were a man who was promising, it would be allowed with impunity to ask for a sign, etc., down to and it would be the punishment of unbelief that he deserved.
1.19: 1.19 Before God. THE SAME. When angels come to us, they fulfil the ministry outwardly in such a way that inwardly they still stand before God through contemplation. For although an angel is a circumscribed spirit, the supreme Spirit who is God is uncircumscribed, and within him the angel runs, wherever he is moved or sent.
1.22: 1.22 And he made signs to them, and remained dumb, etc. Striving to indicate bodily acts without a voice, and not expressing his wish. The people of the Jews is like him, unable to give an account of their deeds.
1.23: 1.23 And it came to pass, after the days were accomplished, etc. Because in the time of their turn the priests of the temple, devoted solely to its duties, abstained not only from the embrace of their wives but even from entering their houses. But for our priests, of whom not fleshly succession but spiritual perfection is sought, who ought to be at hand daily at the altar, perpetual chastity is enjoined.
1.24: 1.24 Hid herself. AMBROSE. She hid herself because she was ashamed of the age of her childbearing, etc., down to for she who was not ashamed of an aged union would not be ashamed of the childbirth.
1.25: 1.25 Thus has he dealt. BEDE. These things were done, says John Chrysostom, etc., down to because through him the affliction of penance was to be preached.
1.26: 1.26 And in the sixth month. JEROME. As in the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent by God into a city of Galilee, so in the sixth millennium Christ was sent, Gabriel. BEDE. Angels are sometimes designated by name so that from the very name it may be shown what they come to minister. Gabriel is the strength of God, because he announces him who was coming to overcome the devil.
1.27: 1.27 To a virgin. A woman seduced by the devil brought in death: on the contrary, a woman instructed by an angel brought forth salvation.
1.28: 1.28 The Lord is with you. She whom he lifted to heavenly things by a new love of chastity, and afterwards, through human nature as mediator, consecrated with all the fullness of divinity. Blessed are you among women. She who, without example of the condition of women, is both virgin and mother, and bore God.
1.29: 1.29 She was troubled, etc. Because she did not know whether what the angel said was past or future.
1.30: 1.30 And the angel said to her: Fear not, Mary. Her who was troubled by the unusual greeting he calls by name, as one known more familiarly. He bids her not to fear, and explains more fully why he called her full of grace.
1.31: 1.31 Jesus. Jesus is said to mean savior, or saving. For he will save, not the people of Israel, but his own people, whether from the foreskin or from circumcision, gathered into one fold under one shepherd.
1.32: 1.32 The throne of David his father. BEDE. That is, the Israelite people, etc., down to in those who, cut from the wild olive, have been grafted into the good olive.
1.35: 1.35 The Holy One shall be called the Son of God. Jesus is born holy, so that he might overcome the condition of corruptible nature, and he was not conceived by the mingling of carnal union. We, bound by the condition of corruptible nature, can be sanctified through grace. And it is fitting that she who conceived as a virgin contrary to custom should bear the Son of God above the custom of human practice.
1.36: 1.36 And behold, etc. BEDE. Lest the virgin despair of the birth, etc., down to she would also learn that the forerunner would be born of a barren old woman. Your cousin. Because she is of the tribe of Levi, that is, of the tribe of God. BEDE. We read that Aaron, who was of the tribe of Levi, etc., down to who, according to God, were not without the fellowship of spiritual kinship.
1.38: 1.38 Behold the handmaid of the Lord. She does not exalt herself from any singular merit, but mindful in all things of her own condition and of her divine kinship, she confesses herself the handmaid of him whose mother she is chosen to be, and with great devotion desires the angel's promise to be fulfilled.
1.39: 1.39 And Mary rising up in those days, went into the hill country with haste into a city of Juda. AMBROSE. Not unbelieving of the oracle, etc., down to where it is added: And it came to pass, when she heard.
1.40: 1.40 And she entered into the house of Zacharias. From this let holy women learn what diligence they owe to their pregnant kinswomen. And saluted Elizabeth. BEDE. She salutes first, because it is fitting that the more chaste one is, the more humble she be.
1.41: 1.41 Leaped, etc. Because he could not with his tongue, he salutes with exulting spirit, and begins the office of his forerunning. Behold, what the angel had said appears: He shall be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb.
1.42: 1.42 Blessed are you. BEDE, AMBROSE. The words of the Gospel agree with the words of the psalm in which David is promised: Of the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne Psalm 131. And with the same voice Mary is blessed by Elizabeth as by Gabriel, so that she may be shown to be venerable to both angels and men, and to be preferred to our women.
1.43: 1.43 The mother of my Lord. I perceive the miracle, I recognize the mystery: the mother of the Lord, made fruitful by the Word, full of God.
1.44: 1.44 For behold, as soon as. At the very moment the voice enters the ears of the body, spiritual power enters the heart of the hearer, and kindles with love of the one who comes not only the mother but also the offspring. Leaped. BEDE. By the revelation of the Spirit with whom she was filled, etc., down to the virgin believed, where the priest denied.
1.46: 1.46 My soul magnifies the Lord. THE SAME. First she professes the gifts spiritually granted to her, etc., down to I spend in observing his commandments.
1.47: 1.47 And my spirit has rejoiced. THE SAME. Because I do not care for earthly things, prosperity does not soften me, adversity does not break me, but only the memory of him delights me, from whom eternal salvation is hoped for; I rejoice in the divinity of him by whose temporal conception my flesh is made fruitful.
1.48: 1.48 For he has regarded. THE SAME. Behold how lowly are the things she thinks of herself, etc., down to and from small and weak ones he makes great and strong ones. For he that is mighty has done great things to me. Because he took flesh in me, and cleansed me from sins, and bestowed on me the gifts of the Holy Spirit. And his mercy. BEDE. From special gifts she turns to the general judgments of God, etc., down to she adds what the proud deserve.
1.53: 1.53 He has filled the hungry with good things. THE SAME. Those who desire eternal things with their whole zeal will be satisfied when Christ appears in glory. But those who rejoice in earthly things are in the end sent away empty of all blessedness. Even in the present we see the humble filled by divine grace, and the proud deprived of the light of truth.
1.55: 1.55 As he spoke to our fathers. Making memory of the fathers to whom this salvation was revealed, she names Abraham expressly, to whom the incarnation itself was first manifested. To his seed for ever. Not so much those begotten in the flesh as those who have followed the footsteps of faith, to whom the coming of the Savior is promised for ever, because the very promise of the inheritance will be closed by no end. For believers will not fail even to the end of the age, and the glory of blessedness will be everlasting.
1.56: 1.56 And Mary abode. BEDE. She stayed so long until she saw the birth of the forerunner, for the sake of which she had chiefly come. Nor did she stay so long for the sake of familiarity alone, but so that in so long a time the progress of both Elizabeth and John might grow. For if at Mary's first coming they were filled with the Holy Spirit, much was added to them by so long a stay.
1.59: 1.59 On the eighth day. By circumcision the resurrection of the Lord is figured, since it too took place on the eighth day, that is, after the sabbath. And as circumcision used to absolve from the guilt of death, so this resurrection both displayed the birth to immortal life in our Author and showed it to be hoped for in us. And they called him. BEDE. The celebrated birth of John is the begun grace of the New Testament, etc., down to it expresses the grace of the Gospel if rightly understood.
1.62: 1.62 And they made signs to his father, etc. Those who make signs to the father about the name of the child signify those who strive to build up the grace of faith by the testimony of the law.
1.67: 1.67 And prophesied, saying. BEDE. Great is the generosity of divine mercy. Behold, the speech which alone was taken away from the one who doubted is restored, together with the spirit of prophecy, to the one who believed.
1.68: 1.68 Blessed. He who, when he asked for the goodness of God, was given a forerunner for the deliverance. He has visited. What he had known was soon to be done, he narrates, in the prophetic manner, as if already done.
1.69: 1.69 A horn of salvation for us. BEDE. By the horn, which projects beyond the flesh although all the bones are covered with flesh, the kingdom of Christ is signified, by which the world and the joys of the flesh are overcome. In figure of which David and Solomon were consecrated to the glory of the kingdom with a horn of oil, as Saul earlier with a flask.
1.71: 1.71 Salvation from our enemies, and from the hand, etc. He has raised up salvation for us from our enemies, and this is an explanation of the previous verse, in which he had briefly said the same: And has raised up a horn of salvation for us.
1.72: 1.72 To perform mercy to our fathers, and to remember his testament, etc. He has spoken, and raised up salvation for us, to perform mercy, so that he may fulfil in us the mercy which he promised to the fathers, and the oath which he swore to the fathers about our deliverance may be accomplished in us through Christ.
1.76: 1.76 And you, child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High: for you shall go before the face of the Lord to prepare, etc. BEDE. It is no wonder if he addresses an infant of eight days, etc., down to whom he recognized that he had taken up as sons.
1.79: 1.79 To direct our feet into the way of peace. And the child grew, etc. That in all things the steps of our works may accord with the grace of our enlightener, until we enter the dwelling of perpetual peace.
2.1: 2.1 There went out a decree from Caesar. AUGUSTINE, BEDE. Augustus reigned in peace for twelve years around the birth of Christ, etc., down to here Judea first became tributary to the Romans.
2.2: 2.2 First. BEDE. At various times already, many parts of the earth are read to have been enrolled, but this is the first of those that embraced the whole world, which is a profession of minds, because no one is excluded. Or at least it began then for the first time, when Cyrinus was sent by Caesar into Syria, to be assessor of estates.
2.4: 2.4 Nazareth. THE SAME. Daily the Lord is conceived in Nazareth, etc., down to that the earnestness of the speaking teacher is worth nothing unless the hearer have received an increase of help from above so as to be heard.
2.6: 2.6 And it came to pass. The Lord willed to be conceived in one place and born in another, so that he might the more easily escape the fury of the plotting Herod. The humility of Christ is commended, because he willed not only to be incarnate but also to be born at that time, so that, as soon as born, he would be subjected to the census of Caesar for our deliverance.
2.7: 2.7 Wrapped him in swaddling clothes. He is clothed in vile cloths, that we might receive the robe of immortality. His hands and feet are bound, that our hands may be directed to working well and our feet into the way of peace; he became a little child, that we might be perfect.
2.8: 2.8 And shepherds. BEDE. With the supreme Shepherd born, the shepherds from the snares of the night, etc., down to upon whom divine grace shines more abundantly.
2.9: 2.9 And behold an angel of the Lord. THE SAME. The citizens of heaven bear witness to the Lord as to be conceived, as conceived, and as born, so that they may sufficiently instruct mortals and render their own service to the Author.
2.12: 2.12 The infant wrapped in swaddling clothes. THE SAME. The infancy of the Savior has been pressed on us by frequent testimonies of both angels and evangelists, so that what he became for us may be fixed more deeply in our minds. In it humility is commended: Though he was rich, he became poor for us, that by his poverty he might enrich us II Cor. 8.
2.14: 2.14 And on earth peace. When by sinning we were strangers to God, the angels counted us strangers; but since we have acknowledged our king, the angels recognized us as their fellow citizens. And the angel fears to be adored by the human nature which he regards in his own king. To men of good will. BEDE. Those who receive Christ born, not those who, on hearing of his birth, were troubled and persecuted him. There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord Isa. 48.
2.16: 2.16 And they came with haste. BEDE. The presence of Christ is not to be sought with sloth, etc., down to as in a manger they will find.
2.17: 2.17 And seeing. It is the vision or knowledge of God, and this alone is the life of men, that they know the true Father, and Jesus Christ whom he sent, to be one God.
2.18: 2.18 They wondered. They wonder both at the mystery of the incarnation and at such a testimony of the shepherds, who did not know how to invent what they had heard, but with simple eloquence proclaimed true things. But the Lord appointed not rhetoricians but fishermen to evangelize. So also in the Old Testament he ordained shepherds as messengers of his dispensation. Therefore the testimony of the shepherds is not to be lightly esteemed.
2.20: 2.20 And they returned, etc. BEDE. So spiritual shepherds now, while others sleep, are borne up by contemplating heavenly things, etc., down to while they say: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will.
2.22: 2.22 They carried him. Little ones who were carried from the whole kingdom of the Jews to the temple, if they were of the tribe of Levi, were kept perpetually for the service of the house. If of another tribe, the firstborn were redeemed by a price given by the parents, to be returned to their own.
2.23: 2.23 As it is written. BEDE. It is written in the law: A woman who having received, etc., down to with the fruits of good works she enters the joys of heavenly blessedness.
2.24: 2.24 A pair of turtledoves. THE SAME. This was the offering of the poor, who could not afford to offer a lamb, so that the humility of the Lord might be evident in all things.
2.25: 2.25 And behold a man. Not only angels, but every age and sex gives testimony to the born child. And as he was foretold by the faithful of all ages, so when he comes he is proclaimed with the praise of all the saints.
2.27: 2.27 The child. Since boyhood begins after the seven years of infancy, Jesus is frequently called a child, not so much because of age as for service, whence the Prophet: Behold my servant, because the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister Isa. 42.
2.29: 2.29 Now you dismiss your servant. AMBROSE. Let whoever wishes to be dismissed come to Jerusalem, etc., down to then he will be dismissed so as not to see death, because he had seen life.
2.34: 2.34 Behold, this child is set. For the fall of those who had stood, and for the resurrection of those who had fallen; or for the fall of vices, and for the resurrection of virtues. He is set for fall and resurrection not only in himself but also in his preachers, whence the Apostle: We are the good odor of Christ to God, in those who are saved, and in those who perish. For by a good odor some are saved, others perish II Cor. 2.
2.35: 2.35 A sword. BEDE. The sorrow of the Lord's passion, etc., down to he sees the cockle sprouting. That may be revealed. Before, it was uncertain which of the Jews would receive the grace of Christ and which would spit upon it; but when the birth was heard of, thoughts are revealed, and Herod and others are troubled, while some come to the teaching of Christ.
2.36: 2.36 And there was Anna, etc. Because the life of the whole world was lost through a man and a woman, in testimony of the life returning through Christ Anna is joined to Simeon. It accords with the mysteries of the Church that Anna means grace, and she is the daughter of Phanuel, who is called the face of God, whence above: The light of your countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us Psalm 4. Of the tribe of Aser. That is, of the blessed, she descended; he is eighth in order of birth among the twelve patriarchs, on account of the mystery of the resurrection. There are five Annas. The first, the mother of Samuel; the second, the wife of Raguel; the third, the mother of Tobias; the fourth, the daughter of Phanuel; the fifth, the mother of Mary. Who was far advanced in days. BEDE. According to the history, Anna, both of devout conduct, etc., down to they are multiplied on account of apostolic teaching.
2.38: 2.38 To all who, etc. To all the faithful who, burdened by the yoke of the foreign Herod, were awaiting the deliverance of the city and the people, she was promising, through the coming of Christ, redemption soon from foreign tyranny.
2.40: 2.40 And the child. BEDE. In that he was a child, etc., down to when he had begun to become man, he was perfect as God.
2.41: 2.41 And his parents went, etc. THE SAME. Rightly is Luke compared to the calf among the four living creatures, etc., down to he concludes at the end of his Gospel with the disciples of the Lord praising in the temple.
2.45: 2.45 And not finding him. THE SAME. If it is asked how he could be forgotten and left behind by his parents, etc., down to that he had returned with the other parent.
2.46: 2.46 In the midst. THE SAME. Like a fountain he sits in the midst of the teachers, but as an example of humility he first asks and listens before he instructs, so that little ones may not be ashamed to be taught by their elders, and the weak may not dare to teach.
2.49: 2.49 How is it that you sought me? THE SAME. He does not rebuke them for seeking him as a son, but suggests who his true Father is, and compels them to lift the eyes of the mind to what they owe rather to him whose eternal Son he is. For because he is God and man, he sets forth now the heights of the Godhead, now the weaknesses of humanity. As Son of God he stays in the temple; as Son of man he goes back with his parents where they command.
2.51: 2.51 And his mother kept all these words in her heart. All that she learned was done concerning the Lord or by the Lord, whether she understood it or could not yet understand it, she stored in memory, so that when the time came to preach or write of his incarnation, she could sufficiently explain everything as it had happened to those who asked. So let us, by frequent meditation on the deeds and words of the Lord, drive off importunate thoughts, and labor to instruct others.
2.52: 2.52 Advanced in wisdom. BEDE. As it is to advance in the age of the flesh, etc., down to that both together might be saved.
3.2: 3.2 The word was made, etc. BEDE. About to gather the Church, the Son of God first works in a little servant, etc., down to and so he said one thing, and declared everything.
3.3: 3.3 Preaching the baptism of penance, etc. THE SAME. John preached the baptism of penance, and gave it to some also, etc., down to he is preceded by his baptism, by which sins cannot be loosed.
3.4: 3.4 The voice of one crying. A voice, because he is the herald of the word. In the desert. Because he announces the consolation of redemption to a desolate and forsaken Judea. No word is heard without a voice, nor does a voice have value without the understanding of the word. Prepare the way of the Lord, etc. He who preaches faith and good works, what else does he do but, for the Lord who is coming, prepare a way to the hearts of the hearers, so that the power of grace may illumine them, and make straight paths for God, while he forms clean thoughts in the mind through the sermon of preaching.
3.5: 3.5 And the crooked shall be. BEDE. The crooked, that is, the hearts of the wicked, twisted through injustice, will be directed to the rule of justice.
3.6: 3.6 And shall see. THE SAME. In this life not every man could see Christ, but on the day of judgment, on the seat of majesty, both elect and reprobate alike will see him, that the just may be rewarded, and the wicked groan for ever. Hence it is added:
3.7: 3.7 Who has shown, etc.? AMBROSE. Who has shown in prudence, with the mercy of God poured in, etc.? down to than which he prophesies to be transferred to the Gentiles.
3.8: 3.8 For I say to you. THE SAME. Those who, having lost the sense of reason, etc., down to they are filled with fruits, they are clothed with leaves.
3.11: 3.11 He who has two. BEDE. The tunic is more necessary for oneself than the cloak, etc., down to but let him share what he has with the poor man.
3.12: 3.12 Publicans. THE SAME. Those who exact public taxes, etc., down to at length they might attain to sharing their own goods with their neighbors.
3.15: 3.15 And as the people thought. THE SAME. Not only were they thinking, etc., down to they do not believe he came through a virgin.
3.16: 3.16 But there shall come. Therefore I baptize with water, because he comes who will baptize with the Spirit, and it is fitting that the way be prepared for him. The latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy. BEDE. I am not worthy to investigate the mystery of the incarnation, etc., down to the evangelical preaching, with which the apostles were shod.
3.19: 3.19 Herod. Before Luke narrates anything of the acts of Jesus, he says that John was seized by Herod, to show that he will describe only those deeds which were done in the year in which John was either seized or punished.
3.21: 3.21 Now Jesus being baptized. BEDE. The Lord is baptized, not needing to be cleansed, etc., down to already taught, he openly proclaims the Son of God.
12.8: 12.8 Everyone who. Lest anyone in the time of persecution think the faith of the heart sufficient for himself, he says: Everyone who confesses. One confesses Jesus with that charity which works through love; one denies him who does not obey the commandments. The Son of man. The Son confesses before the Father the one who has access to the Father through the Son. He is denied by the Son before the Father, to whom the Son and the Father are not manifested in the power of the divinity. And lest the condition be thought the same for all, both for those who deny out of zeal and for those who deny out of weakness or ignorance, he adds: And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of man will be forgiven.
12.10: 12.10 But to him. Even to him who, scandalized by the weakness of the flesh, has suspected me to be a mere man or a glutton, it will be forgivable; but he who, not recognizing the grace of the Holy Spirit (by which repentance is inspired and one returns to the assembly), has remained with an unrepentant heart, since this is now not human but diabolical, it will be unforgivable.
12.11: 12.11 And when they bring you into the synagogues, and before magistrates and authorities. The terror of such assemblies usually takes away freedom of speech. Do not be anxious. Offer your will for Christ. Christ himself will speak for himself.
12.13: 12.13 Teacher. To the one commending the grace of heavenly peace and unity, this man wishes to bring the trouble of earthly division, whence he is also called man, that is, earthly. For among those where such zeal and contention exist, they are men and walk according to man. Among brothers, not a judge as mediator, but piety ought to divide the patrimony as an arbiter, although the patrimony of immortality is not to be sought from men with money.
12.14: 12.14 Who made me. I am not a God of dissension, but of peace and unity, who came to make peace among men and with the angels, that many might have one heart and one soul. Not that they be divided, but that they have all things in common, and that there be no one in need among them. He who does not gather with me is a divider of brotherhood and author of dissension.
12.15: 12.15 From all avarice. No one would think it a crime to divide an inheritance or to gather fruits into barns, but the heavenly judge shows that this too is avarice, whence he adds: of a certain rich man. As above against the Pharisees and hypocrites, so here, on the occasion of a foolish request, he argues against avarice. Not in abundance. Man does not live by bread alone, but by the word of God (Deut. 8), nor is temporal life prolonged by a multitude of riches.
12.16: 12.16 And he said, etc. After the precept he adds an example for avoiding the avarice of temporal things. Of a certain rich man the land brought forth abundantly. The rich man is not blamed for having tilled the land or stored the fruits in barns, but for having placed the confidence of his life in them and not having given to the poor, so as to be received by them into eternal dwellings.
12.17: 12.17 What shall I do, etc. Reckoning his fruits and goods to be his own, he does not give the surplus to the poor, but is intent on reserving it for his luxury in the future, ignorant of who will use what has been gathered.
12.19: 12.19 My goods, and I will say. AMBROSE. Those are not a man's goods which he cannot take with him. For mercy alone is the companion of the dead. Take your rest. Behold, the plague of sloth is joined to the plague of avarice, so that he did not even petition God for temporal things.
12.20: 12.20 But he said. The speaking of God is to restrain a man's perverse schemes by sudden punishment. Fool. Because you promised yourself a long time of riches, this night, snatched away, you will leave to others what you have gathered. They demand, etc. The soul is taken away in the night, which in the darkness of its heart refused to foresee what it could suffer.
12.21: 12.21 And is not rich toward God. He is rich toward God who, despising transitory things, distributes to the poor; whose expectation is the Lord, whose substance, that is, the possession of conscience by which he is sustained and fed, is with God and not in the purses of the earth.
12.22: 12.22 And he said to his disciples. He strengthens the apostles through faith in the hope of eternal things, because there are many whom love of present things and despair of future things make sluggish. Do not be anxious. It would be more perfect to give everything to the poor and make friends from the mammon of iniquity; but since the devotion of faith is often recalled by weakness, he does not forbid foresight, by which bread is prepared in the sweat of the face, but forbids the anxiety which disturbs the mind and calls it back from eternal things.
12.24: 12.24 Consider. The saints are rightly compared to birds, who, having nothing in the world and not laboring, seek eternal things by contemplation alone, already like the angels. How much more. If God's providence supplies what is necessary to birds that do not labor and do not claim common fruits for themselves by any special dominion, it is true that avarice shows itself to be the cause of our want, we who claim common things as though they were our own and envy others.
12.26: 12.26 If then you cannot. If you cannot work even for the increase of your body, which work is the least for God in comparison with spiritual creation, why are you anxious about the other, greater things, that is, about the preservation of the soul.
12.27: 12.27 Consider the lilies. An evident comparison. Lilies, unlike other crops, require no cultivation by farmers. The lily is also often used to signify heavenly blessedness, to which the Lord invites us. Lilies are born not in the woods but in gardens; so we too ought to be born in the gardens of virtues. Not even Solomon. AMBROSE. Solomon is said both here to be clothed and elsewhere to be covered with glory, he who clothed the weakness of bodily nature, as though covered by a certain virtue of mind, with the glory of his works. He clothed as one of these. What purple of kings, what embroidery of weavers can be compared to flowers? The very color is called the garment of the flower, as it is said: Redness covered him.
12.28: 12.28 Tomorrow into the oven. Tomorrow in the Scriptures is used for the future, as Jacob says: My justice will answer me tomorrow (Gen. 30).
12.29: 12.29 Do not seek what you shall eat or what you shall drink. He does not say: Do not seek or be anxious about food or clothing, but more expressly what you shall eat or what you shall drink. In this those seem to be rebuked who, spurning common food or clothing, seek more refined or more austere food or clothing than those with whom they live. Do not be lifted up. Having forbidden anxiety about food and clothing, which are for necessity, he also forbids the pride which usually follows from such superabundance: therefore do not seek these things, because such anxiety makes us like unbelievers.
12.30: 12.30 And all these things. Because all things belong to the children, therefore all these things will be added to you, even without your seeking, so that neither in the present nor in the future may any grace be lacking to the faithful; if these things are withdrawn from them, it is for testing, if given, for thanksgiving, because all things work together for good for the good.
12.32: 12.32 Do not fear. Seek the kingdom, and do not distrust concerning the kingdom; for the Father in his pleasing goodness will give you the kingdom, not by your merits. Little. Either in comparison with the greater number of the reprobate, or rather because of the devotion of humility, by which humility the Church grows, and through which one comes to the kingdom.
12.33: 12.33 Sell. Not only should you not fear that the necessities of life will be lacking to those who fight for the kingdom, but even sell what you possess for the sake of almsgiving, which is the way to the kingdom, since through it sins are redeemed. Not only share your food with the poor, but even sell your possessions, so that, having once despised all you have for the Lord, you may afterward work with the labor of your hands, whence you may live or give alms. Give alms. Let him who for heaven despises all worldly things sell what he has and distribute it; let him who is not of such virtue give alms from what he has. Unfailing. Temporal things either fail by their own fragility, or if anything solid remains, like precious stones, it can be taken by thieves. But what is given for Christ bears eternal fruit in heaven.
12.34: 12.34 For where your treasure is. Universally, both of money and of all pleasures. For the glutton the belly is the treasure, where he has his heart, and so with the others. For if it is on earth, the heart is downward; if in heavenly things, it is fixed in Christ. For it is necessary that where the treasure of love has gone before, there the affection of thought should follow.
12.35: 12.35 Let your loins be girded, etc., and lamps. It does not please God to have one without the other, when someone either does good deeds while luxury is not yet restrained, or lives chastely without exercising himself in good works. And so that you may be removed from the love of temporal things, and do the good things you do with a single intention toward eternal things, gird your loins, that is, restrain the movements of carnal desires, and have burning lamps, so that in your work you may burn with the love of God alone and give an example to others.
12.36: 12.36 Waiting for. Whether you avoid evils or do good, be cleansed of nothing in yourselves, but only wait for the coming of the Redeemer. When he returns. The Lord went to the wedding when, after the resurrection, the new man joined to himself a multitude of angels; he returns from them when he is made manifest to us by judgment. Hence he rightly adds about those who wait: That when he comes, they may open to him at once. He who fears to see angry the one he has despised, and dreads to leave the body, does not wish to open to the judge who knocks. He opens who awaits the judge joyful and secure, and rejoices at approaching death; hence it is added: Blessed are those servants whom, when he comes, etc.
12.37: 12.37 Watching. He watches who keeps his eyes open in the true light, so as to avoid the darkness of negligence; who also does what he has believed, who is careful in the care of the flock committed to him. What is owed to those who watch he adds: Amen I say to you.
12.38: 12.38 And if he comes in the second, etc. He calls them watches by likeness to those who keep guard. In the night of this world we ought always to be wary of the enemy and to wait for the light to come, that is, the coming of the judge. The first watch, then, is the guarding of childhood, the second of youth, the third of old age. If anyone has neglected to watch in childhood, let him not despair, but come to his senses in youth or at least finally in old age, because the merciful judge patiently awaits our delays. To shake off the sluggishness of the mind he brings in the likeness of condemned external things, so that by this the soul may be roused to guard itself. Hence: But know this, that if the master of the house knew. The thief digs through the house when the master does not know, because while the spirit sleeps without guarding itself, unforeseen death of the flesh breaks into the dwelling and drags it off to punishments. But it would resist the thief if it watched, because, foreseeing the judge's coming in secret, it would meet him by doing penance.
12.40: 12.40 At an hour you do not think the Son of man will come. The Lord willed that the last hour always be unknown, so that it may always be suspected and one may always be prepared for it.
12.41: 12.41 And Peter said to him. When the Lord had set forth two things, namely that he would come suddenly and that they ought to be prepared by waiting, Peter asks whether those lofty institutions of the heavenly life, which are necessary for those preparing themselves, pertain only to the apostles and those like them, or to all who are to be saved.
12.42: 12.42 And the Lord said. Answering the questions, the Lord says that the first and the second judgment will be present to all, and that individuals will be either rewarded or condemned according to their merits. Then, what Peter had chiefly asked, he adds, namely that the grace of the virtues which he had brought to the world is to be pursued by each as far as possible, which is where: I came to cast fire upon the earth. Who do you think is the faithful steward? As if to say: To you, who are appointed stewards, this applies more especially, concerning watchfulness and preparation, that you may prepare both yourselves and others for the judge's coming, because few are those who well administer the stewardship committed to them. And wise, whom the Lord has set over his household, that, etc. How rare is he who serves the Lord for the Lord's sake, feeding the sheep of Christ not for gain but out of love of Christ, wise for the future, providing for himself, whom he appointed; that is, how rare is he who is called by God like Aaron, and has not rather thrust himself in, and who does not feed himself more than the sheep!
12.43: 12.43 Blessed. As if to say: The faithful are few. But he who is found faithfully dispensing the measure of the word, and watching in the care of the flock, will be glorified with eternal blessedness.
12.44: 12.44 Over all that he possesses. As great as is the distance of merits between good hearers and good teachers, so great also is that of rewards. He makes the good hearers sit at table and, passing by, serves them; he sets the stewards over all that he possesses, not that they alone may have eternal things, but that they may have them beyond the rest, both for their own life and for guarding the flock.
12.45: 12.45 But if that servant says. Note that among the servant's vices is counted that he thinks the master's return slow. Among the virtues of the good it is not counted that they hoped for it soon, but only that they ministered faithfully. Nothing then is better than to bear patiently not knowing what cannot be known, yet to labor that we may be found fit. And to eat. That is, to be occupied with all the crimes and enticements of the world, which make the mind go astray, or literally, if he is given to gluttony and drunkenness.
12.46: 12.46 And a portion. The wicked will be punished with the unbelievers, but differently. For those who sin knowingly will be punished more severely; less severely those who sin from ignorance. And among the unjust each will have a more tolerable damnation the less iniquity he had.
12.48: 12.48 Few. The mildest punishment of all is theirs who, besides original sin, have added no further offense. AMBROSE. Many, thinking they will be beaten less if they do not know, etc., up to but they are judged contemptuous. But to everyone. Rightly the wicked man who knows more, and the one who does not know, less, will be beaten, because more was entrusted to the one, less to the other; and from everyone to whom more is entrusted, more is required.
12.49: 12.49 Fire, etc. As if to say: You were asking whether I am admonishing all to await the Lord's coming with girded loins and burning lamps? But I, who came into the world only for this, to kindle men from the desires of the world to heavenly things, want nothing else but that the radiance of this fire may illumine all parts of the world until the end of the age, and that it may so blaze in the hearts of the faithful that it is not extinguished by any onrush of waves or winds. But I have a baptism, etc. And that this fire may be kindled in the hearts of the faithful, so that they can perfectly despise all temporal things and themselves, I must first be baptized with a baptism, that is, be bathed with the anointing of my own blood; for the Spirit would not be given unless Jesus were first glorified. And how. So great is the Lord's condescension that he testifies that within him is zeal for pouring devotion into us, for completing perfection in us, and for hastening the passion on our behalf; he who, having nothing in himself to grieve over, was yet distressed by our miseries, and at the time of death displayed a sorrow which he had taken up not from fear of his own death but from the delay of our redemption. Until it is accomplished. He who is distressed up to perfection is secure of the perfection, and is not distressed about it itself; rather the death of the body is the release of anxiety, not a heaping up of sorrow.
12.51: 12.51 Do you think. How, after the baptism of the passion and after the coming of the fire, the earth will burn, he says: Because the whole world was divided against itself over faith in Christ, each house had believers and unbelievers, the one fighting against the faith, the other for the faith.
12.52: 12.52 In one house. Every man is one house, either of God or of the devil. Thus a spiritual man is a spiritual house. Divided. The first cause is that of religion toward God, the second that of piety toward neighbor. For it is necessary that you put human things after divine. We must not therefore renounce our loved ones, but God must be preferred to all. For the pledges of nature are gifts of God, and the gift that is received ought not to be loved more than God, by whom the gift received is preserved. Three against two. That is, son and daughter and daughter-in-law against father and mother; and two against three, that is, father and mother, where the mother-in-law is also understood, against son and daughter and daughter-in-law.
12.54: 12.54 And he said. When he had instructed even the apostles about his first coming, hinting at what was done in it, and had admonished them about the future, how they ought to await him, he turns his speech to the crowds, among whom were Pharisees, as Matthew indicates: because they neither believed the first coming had happened nor rightly awaited the second, and sought a sign from heaven, tempting him. These therefore he rebukes, because if they were willing to attend, they could have from the words of the prophets a sure indication of both comings. When you see. Mystically: The cloud rising from the west signifies the flesh of Christ rising again from death, from which time the rain of the Gospel preaching has been poured upon all lands. The south wind blowing before the heat signifies lighter tribulations before the judgment. A shower comes. Literally the sense is clear: Those who can foreknow the state of the breezes from the change of the elements could also know the time of both comings, both from the sayings of the prophets and from the magnificence of his works.
18.29: 18.29 No one. He who has left carnal things for the Lord will receive spiritual things. Mark says: A hundredfold now, etc. (Mark 10), that is, in this life, full of persecutions, they taste the joy of the kingdom and enjoy the sincere love of all the elect.
18.30: 18.30 Shall receive, etc. He who for the Lord has left all riches and despised the affections of the flesh will receive much more in the present, and from brothers and sisters bound by the spiritual glue of his purpose he will receive a far more gracious charity in this life.
18.31: 18.31 He took. Foreseeing that the disciples would be troubled by his passion, he foretells both the pain of the passion and the glory of the resurrection, so that when they saw him dying they would not doubt he would rise. And will be accomplished. In this he shows that whatever the prophets foretold was directed to the mystery of his dispensation. In this he strikes the heretics, who say that Christ preached what was contrary to the law and the prophets, and that the God of the Old Testament is one, of the New another. He also refutes the madness of the pagans, since they deride his cross, whereas he showed the time of his coming passion as one foreknowing the future, and approached the place as one not fearing death.
18.34: 18.34 And they, etc. The disciples, though the word of the Lord's passion was repeated so often, are unable to understand it, because they cannot bear to hear the death of him whom they most desire to see, and they do not think he can die whom they know to be not only an innocent man but also true God.
18.35: 18.35 A blind man. The blind man signifies the human race, which, shut out from heavenly brightness, suffers the darkness of its condemnation, but is healed by the Lord as he draws near to Jericho. Jericho is interpreted moon, by which the waning of mortality is understood. While the Word of God takes up the weakness of our flesh, man returns to knowing things. The blind man sits by the way when he begins to believe in him who says: I am the way (John 14). He begs, while he prays.
18.39: 18.39 And those who went before, etc. Those who go before Jesus as he comes signify the blindness of carnal vices, which scatter the thought of man and disturb the voice of prayer, so that Jesus cannot come to illumine the heart of man; but he, now feeling himself burdened by the phantoms of former vices, and the voice of his prayer hindered so that he cannot be heard for himself, cries out more ardently.
18.40: 18.40 And Jesus standing, etc. Passing by, he hears the blind man; standing, he enlightens him, because through his humanity he sympathizes with the voices of our blindness, but through the power of the Godhead he pours the light of grace into us. To be brought to him. He who in some measure sensed him passing by, while in prayer he suffers the crowds of phantoms, pressing on more vehemently in prayer is led to him standing, and receives light, because God is fixed in a firm heart, and so the lost light is restored.
18.41: 18.41 What do you want, etc. He does not ask out of ignorance, but so as to be asked, to stir the mind to prayer. Understanding this, the blind man adds: Lord, that I may see. The blind man does not ask for gold or anything temporal, but only light. Let us then imitate him whom we have heard healed in mind and body; let us ask of the Lord the light of the eternal vision, and he will say to us: Receive your sight, your faith has made you well.
18.43: 18.43 And immediately he saw. He sees and follows who does the good he understands, and imitates Jesus present or passing by. And such a man not only advances toward God by what he obtained but also kindles others to the praise of God. And all the people. The people praise God not only for the gift of light obtained but also for the merit of the faith of him who obtained it, because they praise not only that he enlightens powerfully and mercifully, but that he hears the cry of one who cries out in firm faith.
19.1: 19.1 And entering, etc. Behold, the camel, having laid down the burden of the hump, passes through the eye of a needle, when, having despised the wealth of frauds, he ascends the narrow gate which leads to life. And because by devotion of faith he makes up, by climbing a tree, for what nature gave him too little of to see the Savior, he justly receives the blessing of the Lord's reception which he desired but did not dare to ask. Mystically, Zacchaeus, which is interpreted justified, signifies the believers from the Gentiles who were weighed down by the occupation of temporal things, and were the least, but were sanctified by the Lord. And he was rich. Who would despair of himself, when this man comes to God whose wealth was from fraud? Through him it appears that not every rich man is avaricious.
19.3: 19.3 Because of the crowd. What is the crowd but the confusion of the unlearned multitude, which cannot see the summit of wisdom? Zacchaeus, then, not in the crowd but having passed beyond the common people, beholds the Messiah whom he desires.
19.4: 19.4 A sycamore. The sycamore is a tree, like the mulberry in its leaves but outstanding in height, and is interpreted foolish fig, that is, the cross. It feeds believers like a fig, and is mocked by unbelievers as foolish. How small he climbs, when any humble person, aware of his own weakness, glories in the power of the cross, and through this praiseworthy foolishness sees the Lord passing near, because, though not yet so solidly as he now does, yet in haste, and as if in passing, he fixes his attention on the light of heavenly wisdom. For he was to pass that way. ISIDORE. That part where the sycamore was, or where he was to believe, etc., up to as it were in the fruitful height of work he stood out.
19.5: 19.5 And when he came. Through the heralds of his word sent before, in whom Jesus was and spoke, he came to the people of the nations, who, already lifted up by faith in his passion, burns also to acknowledge his divinity; looking up he sees, because he has chosen the one who was raised from earthly things through faith and chose him, and loves the one who loves him. Come down. That he is commanded to come down from the sycamore, and so to prepare a dwelling in his house, is what the Apostle says: Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer. For if he died from weakness, yet he now lives by the power of God (2 Cor. 5, 13). To stay. The Lord sometimes stayed in the house of the leader of the Pharisees, that is, he taught in the Synagogue of the Jews.
19.7: 19.7 They murmured. It is manifest that the Jews always hated the salvation of the Gentiles, or did not understand it. Hence it is also said against Peter: Why did you go in to the uncircumcised Gentiles? (Acts 9).
19.8: 19.8 And standing, etc. While others slander him as a sinful man, Zacchaeus himself, standing, that is, persisting in the truth of the faith he had begun, proves not only that he was converted from a sinner but also that he had lived among the innocent, since even before conversion he lived innocently, and he who before conversion could give half can after conversion give the whole. If anything, etc. The first thing is to restore according to the law, then to give what remains to the poor. This fruit of life the publican gathers from the sycamore through wise foolishness: he restores what was taken, leaves what is near, despises what is visible, and longs to follow the footsteps of him whom he does not yet see.
19.9: 19.9 A son. Not by flesh but by faith, because as Abraham at God's command left his country for the hope of a future inheritance, so this man also acquires a treasure in heaven by hope.
19.10: 19.10 Came, etc. Even to those who murmur he does not disdain to explain his mysteries: that he himself came to earth chiefly to look upon the repentance of sinners, where he also calls himself the Son of man, that he may make known to us the dispensation of his mercy.
19.11: 19.11 As they heard these things, etc. Having received and commended the repentance of the rich publican, he teaches by a parable that the repentance of sinners pleases him more than the righteousness of the proud, and that he will reign more widely among the Gentiles, humble in their ignorance of the law, than among the Jews, proud of the righteousness of the law. Because. Not only those who persevere as just but also those who are converted from injustice belong to the children of the promise.
19.12: 19.12 A nobleman went. This is the nobleman to whom the blind man cried: Have mercy on me, Son of David, and to whom the trumpets cried: Hosanna to the Son of David: blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the king of Israel, who was appointed king by the Father, to whom the nations were given as an inheritance. Far country. Leaving the blinded Jews, he goes to enlighten the Gentiles, who cry to the Lord from far off (because from the ends of the earth), or because salvation is far from sinners (Ps. 118): God, who is present everywhere, is far from those who worship idols, but they too have been made near in the blood.
19.13: 19.13 And having called ten. He calls ten servants, when he chose disciples steeped in the letter of the Decalogue. He gives ten minas, when after the resurrection he rises and opens their understanding, that they may understand spiritually the sayings of the law. The mina weighs ten drachmas. And every word of Scripture, because it suggests the perfection of the heavenly life, shines as with the weight of the number one hundred. Trade. Offer to the peoples the words of the law, examined by mystical interpretation, and receive from them confession of faith and uprightness of conduct.
19.15: 19.15 And it came to pass. Daily Christ, having received the kingdom from the Father, returns, because he always beholds the state of the Church on pilgrimage on earth. To this servant he lends money to trade with; in the other he examines the measure of the work accomplished. This one, laboring prudently, he endows with greater grace; that one, pursuing luxurious things, he deprives even of what he had given. In the judgment, however, many who seemed fit for teaching will, on account of their negligence, be reckoned among the unlearned. Some of simpler observance, by their devotion, will receive among the apostolic the highest rewards. For he who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet's reward (Matt. 10).
19.16: 19.16 And the first came. The first servant is the order of teachers sent in the circumcision, who received one mina to trade with, because he was sent to preach one God, one faith, one baptism. But he gains ten, when by teaching he associates to himself the people placed under the law.
19.17: 19.17 You were faithful in a little. Whatever gifts we receive in the present is little in comparison with the future ones. For we know in part, and we prophesy in part (1 Cor. 13). Ten cities. The ten cities are souls, coming through the words of the law to the grace of the Gospel, over whom then is set, to be glorified, he who has worthily commended to God the money of the word; hence the Apostle: What is our hope, or joy, or crown of glory? Is it not you, before the Lord Jesus? (1 Thess. 2).
19.18: 19.18 And the second. The good order, about to call the Gentiles and to send to be slain the Jews who did not want Christ to reign over them, set forth this comparison first, lest it be said: He had given the people of the Jews nothing by which it could become better, so that something is demanded of one who receives nothing? From one mina he makes five, he who has moral teaching on account of the five senses.
19.20: 19.20 And another, etc. He who was sent to the uncircumcision, to whom the Lord entrusted for preaching one mina, the very same faith which was entrusted to the circumcision. It makes five minas, because it converts to the grace of the evangelical faith the Gentiles enslaved to the five senses of the body. In a napkin, etc. He stores the money in a napkin who, fit for preaching, either refuses to take up the office of preaching, or does not perform well the office he has taken up, but hides the gifts received in the leisure of time, saying to himself: Is it enough for me to render an account of myself; why should I preach to others, or be compelled to render an account for others? Though before God even those to whom the law was not given are inexcusable, nor did they sleep through the hearing of the Gospel, because through creation they could know the Creator.
19.21: 19.21 You reap what. For God reaps where he has not sown, that is, he holds guilty of impiety even those to whom he did not minister the word of the law or the Gospel. Fearing therefore the danger of judgment, I will rest from the administration of the word.
19.22: 19.22 You knew, etc. What he had thought he said by way of excuse is turned into guilt. If you knew me so harsh and cruel, why did this thought not strike fear into you, so that you would know I would seek what is mine the more diligently?
19.23: 19.23 The money. That is, the evangelical preaching, and you did not make it known to the prepared hearts of the faithful. My, to the table. Not yours. Hence the Apostle: If anyone speaks, let it be as the words of God (1 Pet. 4). With interest. He who buys the money of the word from the teacher by believing must pay with interest by working. Or, he pays interest on the loan of the word received who, from what he hears, strives to understand other things as well.
19.24: 19.24 Take away, etc. He loses the grace conferred who neglected to share it with others by preaching. But it is increased for him who labored in it. As the royal anointing which Saul lost by pride, David deserved by obedience. For the Spirit of the Lord, which departed from Saul, was directed from that day forward to David.
19.26: 19.26 And he shall have abundance. Mystically: when all Israel will be saved, then the fullness of spiritual grace, which we now exercise sluggishly, will be abundantly conferred on the teachers of that time.
19.28: 19.28 And having said these things. The parable finished, he goes to Jerusalem, to show that the parable had been set forth concerning the fate of that same great city, which not long after, about to kill him for hatred of his reign, would perish by hostile slaughter.
19.29: 19.29 To Bethphage. Bethphage is a village of priests on the Mount of Olives, and is interpreted house of the mouth. Bethany is a village or town on the side of the same mount, and is called house of obedience. The Lord, about to come to Jerusalem, exalted these by his presence, because before his passion by teaching he filled many with the gifts of pious confession and spiritual obedience. These are well placed on the Mount of Olives, that is, in the Lord himself, who refreshes us by the anointing of spiritual chrisms and by the light of conscience and piety. And because he does not wish the city set upon a hill to be hidden, he sends the disciples into the village opposite them, that through them he may penetrate the fortifications of the whole world set against him.
19.30: 19.30 Entering you will find. The preachers entering the world find the people of the nations, entangled in the bonds of unbelief, free and wanton. On which no one, etc., that is, no rational teacher has put the bridle of correction, to restrain the tongue from evil or to compel it to go into the narrow way of life. No one gave the garments of salvation by which it might be warmed, by persuading what is useful. No one sat on it, because no one corrected its folly by checking it. Tied. Tied by the bonds of unbelief, in which, bound over or constrained, it served its lord in error, but could not claim lordship for itself, whom it had made lord not by nature but by fault. And therefore when the Lord is spoken of, one is acknowledged. For although there are many gods and lords, yet generally there is one God and one Lord.
19.33: 19.33 And as they were loosing, etc. Do not despise this little ass, because just as among the clothing of sheep are ravening wolves, so beneath the exuviae of the body (which is common to us with beasts) a mind full of God is quickened. They said. He had many lords, who, not devoted to one superstition, was carried off at will by unclean spirits to various errors. Why do you loose. Those who had objected to the loosing of the colt are quiet when they hear the name, because the masters of errors, who oppose the teachers coming for the salvation of the Gentiles, defend their darkness until, with miracles bearing witness, the power of the true possessor stands out. But after the power of the Lord's faith appears, the complaints of the adversaries yielding, a company that carries God in its heart is brought.
19.35: 19.35 Garments. The garments of the apostles are the teaching of virtues, or the discernment of the Scriptures, and spiritual grace, with which they cover the hearts of men, previously naked and cold, that they may deserve to have Christ as rider. They put. While the people of the Gentiles carry Christ, the disciples spread garments in the way, because, stripping off the covering of their body, they prepare the way for the simple with their blood, that with unhindered step of mind they may press on to Jerusalem, where Christ leads, that is, to the true vision of peace.
19.37: 19.37 At the descent. As the Lord descends from the Mount of Olives, that is, as he who was in the form of God humbles himself to the weakness of our flesh, the crowds descend with him, that is, those who need his mercy are humbled, that they may be exalted by him. Rejoicing. He had often entered the city of Jerusalem, but was not called king, which he had always avoided, except now when he goes up to suffer. This was done so that he might the more stir up their envy against himself, because the time of the passion was now at hand. For. Especially for the resurrection of Lazarus, which had recently happened. For the crowd also came to meet him for this reason, because they had heard he had done this sign. They praise him also for the signs and teaching which he did when he went up to the feast of Tabernacles, which John narrates.
19.38: 19.38 Blessed. The crowd, soon to crucify him, calls him king, and declares that the son of David expected according to the flesh has come, so that testimony against themselves is wrung from the unwilling. Peace. As at the Lord's birth the heavenly hosts of men and angels sang: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men, etc., so men sing to the same one, soon to triumph: Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest.
19.39: 19.39 Teacher. Wonderful is the madness of the envious: they who knew he taught truly, when they hear him called teacher, think his disciples should be rebuked, as though they themselves were better instructed, though those disciples had been instructed by him who is shown by miracles to be God.
19.40: 19.40 Stones. When the Lord was crucified and the apostles were silent for fear, the rocks which were split, the tombs being opened, openly cried out that he was God and Lord of the world. Mystically: if blindness has befallen Israel so that it falls silent from praising God, the people of the Gentiles, their stony heart softened, will believe in their Creator and proclaim him.
19.44: 19.44 And they will not leave. For the perverse man, when he adds perversion, as it were builds stone upon stone. But when the soul is seized for punishment, such a construction of thoughts is scattered, and this because you did not know the time. For God visits the perverse soul, sometimes by a precept, sometimes by a miracle. But because the proud man despises it and is not ashamed of his evils, at the last he will be handed over to enemies, with whom he is gathered in fellowship in the eternal judgment of damnation. For peace, etc. While you give the flesh to pleasures, not foreseeing the coming evils, you have present goods which can be for temporal peace. And why this, he adds, namely because he does not foresee the evils that will befall him. For if he foresaw, he would not have rejoiced in present prosperity.
19.45: 19.45 And entering. After enumerating the evils, entering the temple he cast out those who sold and bought, thereby hinting that the ruin of the people was chiefly from the fault of the priests; for when he strikes those who sell and buy, he shows whence the root of perdition proceeded.
19.47: 19.47 And he was teaching. The house of God is the conscience of the faithful, which those make a den of thieves who, having left the simplicity of holiness, plan to do that by which they can harm an innocent neighbor. But on the contrary the Lord instructs the minds of the faithful to avoid evils. They sought to destroy him. They could not destroy him because they feared the tumult of the people, or they wished to destroy him because, with their own teaching neglected, they saw the whole people flocking to his doctrine.
20.2: 20.2 By what authority. They doubt about the power of God, and wish it to be understood that what he does is the devil's. Hence they add: Or who is it, etc. In which they plainly deny the Son of God, whom they believe to work signs not by his own powers but by another's.
20.3: 20.3 I will ask you, etc. He could have refuted the slander of the tempters by a plain answer, but he prudently asks a question, that they may be condemned either by their silence or by their own judgment.
20.4: 20.4 The baptism of John, etc. He whom you confess to have had prophecy from heaven gave testimony to me, and you heard from him by what authority I act. Understanding this, they hesitate over what they should answer. Neither do I, etc. For two reasons the truth must be hidden from those who ask. Either because they are less able to hear it; hence it is said: I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now (John 16). Or because they ask from hatred and contempt; hence it is said: Do not give what is holy to dogs (Matt. 7).
20.9: 20.9 And he began. The chief priests and scribes having been refuted on their question, the Lord pursues what he had begun, and, with them listening, addresses the people, who hear his words more willingly, bringing in a parable by which he both convicts them of impiety and shows that the kingdom of God is to be transferred to the Gentiles. A vineyard. Morally: The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel (Isa. 5); the tenants are the workers hired at the first hour, the third, the sixth and the ninth to cultivate it. And himself abroad, etc. He who is everywhere is more present to those who love him, absent from the negligent, and he was absent a long time, lest the exaction seem unjust. For the more indulgent the generosity, the more inexcusable the obstinacy.
20.10: 20.10 And at the time. The first servant who is sent is Moses the lawgiver. For forty years he sought from the tenants the fruit of the law he had given, but they sent him away beaten and empty.
20.11: 20.11 And he added, etc. The second servant is David the prophet, who after Moses invited the tenants of the vineyard to the exercise of good work with the melody of the psalm and the sweetness of the harp, but they sent him away empty too, treated with contempt, saying: What portion have we in David, or what inheritance in the son of Jesse? (1 Kings 12). Yet he entreats for this vineyard that it may not be utterly uprooted: O Lord God of hosts, turn, look down from heaven, and see and visit this vineyard (Ps. 77). The third servant is the choir of prophets. They rebuked the people and foretold the evils that threatened the vineyard, but those too they persecuted and killed.
20.14: 20.14 And when they saw him. He proves openly that the Jews crucified the Son of God not through ignorance but through envy. For they understood that this was he to whom it was said: Ask of me and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession (Ps. 117). And therefore, taking counsel for themselves, they say: Behold, the whole world has gone after him (John 12), etc. The inheritance of the Church, therefore, which the Father did not leave by dying, but which he himself bought by his death and possessed by rising, this the Jews wish to snatch away, while they try to extinguish the faith which is through him, not subject to the righteousness of God but wishing to establish their own. This is the heir: Christ the heir, because he outlived his own death, and as heirs gathers the profits of the testaments which he himself made, in our advances.
20.15: 20.15 And casting him out. Mark changes the order: They killed him and cast him out of the vineyard (Mark 12). In this their obstinacy is noted, who after the resurrection had been unwilling to believe the apostles preaching, but, casting him away as a useless corpse, gave him to the Gentiles to be received.
20.16: 20.16 God forbid. They contradict the sentence which they know was spoken against their perfidy. For they understand that what they were bearing in mind is contained in the parable. Since the Jews deny, therefore, that it would be just for the divine knowledge of the law (which they themselves despised) to be transferred to the Gentiles, note what the Savior answers.
20.17: 20.17 What is this, etc. How will this prophecy be fulfilled? Only because Christ, rejected by you, is to be preached to the Gentiles who are to believe, so that in himself, the one cornerstone, he may join the two walls. The builders. Those called tenants above are here called builders, because those who were commanded to cultivate the people to bear fruit were also commanded to set it up as a house worthy of the Lord himself as inhabitant.
20.18: 20.18 Everyone who falls. He who believes and yet sins falls upon the stone and is not ground to powder but broken, because through patience he is reserved for salvation. But he on whom the stone falls, that is, who denies utterly, is ground to powder, so that not even a potsherd remains. Or he falls upon it who now despises and does injuries, and has not yet perished utterly but is shattered, so that he does not walk upright. The stone falls upon him whom, coming in judgment, it crushes.
20.19: 20.19 And they sought, etc. They seek to kill him as a liar, in whom what he had said is proved true. For he is the heir; those wicked tenants are held back only by human terror until his hour came.
20.20: 20.20 And watching. What they cannot do themselves for fear of the people, they wish to accomplish with empty devices, so that they may seem free from his death.
20.22: 20.22 Is it lawful for us, etc. When Judea had recently, under Augustus, been made tributary to the Romans, the Pharisees, who applauded themselves for righteousness and gave tithes and firstfruits to God, denied that tribute was to be paid to a man; for which sedition afterward the kingdom and the whole country were destroyed.
20.24: 20.24 Whose has it, etc. The image of God is one, the image of the world another. If then Christ did not have the image of Caesar, why did he pay the tax? He did not give from his own, but rendered to the world what was the world's. And you, if you do not wish to be liable to Caesar, do not have what belongs to the world. If you have riches, you are liable to Caesar. If you wish to owe nothing to the earthly king, leave all your things and follow Christ. And well does he first decree that what is Caesar's must be rendered. For no one can be the Lord's unless he has first renounced the world.
20.25: 20.25 Render therefore. As Caesar demands the impression of his image, so God demands the soul, signed with the light of his countenance.
20.27: 20.27 And there came, etc. There were two heresies among the Jews: that of the Pharisees, who preferred the righteousness of traditions and observances, whence they were also called divided by the people; and that of the Sadducees, who also claimed for themselves what they were not, that is, just.
20.28: 20.28 Teacher. Those who do not believe in the resurrection of bodies, and think that souls perish with bodies, invent a shameful tale, which convicts of folly those who assert the resurrection. It may be, however, that this once happened in their nation. That he may take, etc. Under the law of the letter one was compelled to marry in this life. But under the law of the spirit chastity is commended.
20.35: 20.35 But they, etc. Although all, good and bad, will rise and remain without marriage, the Lord, to rouse to the glory of the resurrection, speaks only of the elect. But if in the resurrection they neither marry wives, then bodies will rise that can marry and take wives. This is said of those who have the genital members, but will be bound by no pleasure or necessity of marrying. And note that though he speaks the secret mysteries to those who lie in wait for him and trample on him, he does not give what is holy to dogs, but there were present many fit persons who ought not to be neglected on account of the uncleanness of others. Nor marry, etc. Since marriages are for the sake of children, children for succession, succession because of death, where there is no death, there are no marriages.
20.37: 20.37 But that the dead rise. After satisfying the proposed question about the conditions of the resurrection, he deals with the resurrection itself against their unbelief.
20.40: 20.40 And they no longer, etc. Refuted in their words, they no longer question him, but openly seize him and hand him over to Roman power, from which we understand that the poisons of envy can indeed be overcome, but hardly rest.
20.41: 20.41 How do they say, etc. The Lord, about to complete the precepts, at the end of his testament concludes with the faith, that we may believe the Lord Jesus, true God and true man, to sit at the right hand of the Father.
20.43: 20.43 Until I make. That the enemies are subjected by the Father signifies not the weakness of the Son but the unity of nature, by which he works in the other in a different way. For the Son also subjects enemies to the Father, because he glorifies the Father on earth.
20.46: 20.46 Beware of the scribes. For a twofold reason we are commanded to beware of those who crave vain glory, lest we be deceived by their pretense, or be inflamed by their example to the love of temporal things. And they love greetings in the marketplace. He does not forbid being greeted in the marketplace, nor the first seats, to those to whom they are due by the order of office, but to those who love them unduly. For he rebukes the disposition, not the rank. Nor is he free of fault if he who desires to sit in the chair of Moses wishes to take part in the lawsuits of the marketplace. Who devour, etc. Mark: Under pretense of long prayer, those who, to appear more religious, pray at greater length, where from any weak persons troubled by the conscience of their sins they receive, as patrons, praises and money, their prayer becomes sin, so that not only can they not intercede for others, but cannot even profit themselves for salvation; rather, for those very prayers they will be more condemned. These will receive condemnation. In this he implies that even those who pray standing in the corners to be seen by men deserve condemnation, but these a greater one.
21.1: 21.1 And looking up, etc. He who had warned that seekers of the first place and of vain glory are to be beware of, also distinguishes with sure examination those bringing gifts into the house of the Lord, that he may reward each according to the intention of the heart.
21.4: 21.4 Out of their abundance. The Jew gives out of abundance, who, presuming on his righteousness, prays thus within himself (Luke 18): God, I thank you that I am not like other men. The Church puts all her living into the gifts of God, and understands that all she suggests is not of her own merit but of the divine gift, saying: God, be merciful to me a sinner.
21.5: 21.5 And some. After the offering of the widow, in which the Church from the Gentiles is signified, the destruction of the temple is added, so that the hidden sacraments of the Church, under the veil of the concealing letter, may begin to lie open. For God took care to overturn the city and the temple and all the figurative things, lest anyone after the coming of Christ should return to them.
21.7: 21.7 They asked. Because to those praising the buildings of the temple he had foretold that all would be destroyed, the disciples (as Mark says) Peter, James, John and Andrew ask privately the time and the signs of the predicted destruction.
21.8: 21.8 For many. With the destruction of Jerusalem imminent, there were many leaders who said they were Christs and that the time of liberty was drawing near. In the times of the apostles also many heresiarchs appeared, who among other falsehoods preached that the day of the Lord was at hand, whom the Apostle also refutes.
