21.9: 21.9 Wars and seditions. These abounded in Judea from the Lord's passion, and the apostles are warned not to be frightened and desert Jerusalem and Judea, because the end is not at once but after the forty-second year.
21.10: 21.10 Then he said. Of these some are from heaven, some from earth, some from the elements, some from men. Mystically: kingdom against kingdom, and the pestilence of those whose speech creeps like a cancer, and the famine of hearing the word of God, the shaking of the earth, must be understood as separation from the true faith in heretics, who by fighting against each other bring about the victory of the Church. And great signs. These too are found fulfilled at that time in Josephus, who narrates that a star like a sword hung over Jerusalem for a year, and that chariots and armed horsemen fought in the air for forty days, and that a heifer between the hands of those sacrificing gave birth to a lamb.
21.13: 21.13 And it shall turn out, etc. Of those who either persecute or are not changed by living. For the death of the just is a help to the good and a testimony of condemnation to the wicked, so that the perverse perish without excuse from the very thing from which the elect take an example to live.
21.16: 21.16 By parents, etc. The torment is greater when one suffers from those on whom he had counted, because with the loss of the body the evils of lost charity torture. And because what is predicted about the affliction of death is hard, a consolation is added about the joy of the resurrection.
21.18: 21.18 And a hair. As if to say: Why do you fear that what hurts when cut will perish, since not even there can what does not hurt when cut perish in you? For flesh when cut hurts, a hair does not hurt.
21.19: 21.19 In your patience. Patience is the root and guardian of all virtues. In it, therefore, we possess our souls, which possess the body, when we rule the souls themselves by reason to suffer. True patience is to bear others' evils with equanimity; to be moved by no pain against him who inflicts evils.
21.21: 21.21 And those who are in the countryside. Ecclesiastical history relates that the Christians who were in Judea, when destruction was imminent, were warned by an angel and dwelt beyond the Jordan in the city of Pella until the desolation of Judea was fulfilled.
21.23: 21.23 For there will be distress, etc. This distress and wrath continues to this day upon that people dispersed through all nations. Yet it will not last forever.
21.24: 21.24 Until they are fulfilled, etc. That is, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, and so all Israel will be saved (Rom. 11), and will return as if to rejoice at the throne of its own birth. For what follows when the times of the nations are fulfilled and all Israel saved, the Lord sets out in order. For according to Matthew the apostles also asked these things, not only the time of the overthrow of the temple but also the sign of his coming and of the consummation of the age.
21.25: 21.25 And there will be signs. These are about the coming itself, when all the virgins, wise and foolish, roused by an unaccustomed cry, trim their lamps, that is, reckon up the works they have with them, for which with the greatest fear they now await the event of the imminent eternal decision. As the last judgment approaches, the sound of the sea and the waves is confounded, and the circle of the lands is infected, the inhabitants pressing on all sides: the greatest lights of heaven, their rays struck with new horror, veil their troubled face, because as their end approaches, the elements as if in dread totter and roar.
21.27: 21.27 And then they will see. Him whom they refused to hear in humility, that they may then feel his power the more strictly, as now they do not incline their hearts to his patience. But because these things were said against the reprobate, he soon adds for the consolation of the elect.
21.28: 21.28 But when these things begin to happen. That is, when the plagues multiply, when the terror of judgment is shown with the powers shaken. Lift up your heads. Cheer your hearts, because, while the world comes to an end, to which you are not friends, the redemption you seek is near. That the world ought to be despised is made plain by a foresighted comparison.
21.29: 21.29 See the fig tree. He compares the kingdom of God to summer, because then the clouds of our sorrow will pass, and the eternal days of life will shine under the brightness of the sun. For as from the fruit of trees the nearness of summer is known, so also from the ruin of the world the kingdom of God is known to be near. From these words it is shown that the fruit of the world is ruin. For it grows to fall, it buds so that whatever it has budded it consumes in calamities.
21.33: 21.33 Heaven and earth. Nothing in the nature of bodies is more lasting than heaven and earth. Nothing passes more swiftly than speech. Words, so long as they are incomplete, are not words; if they are complete, they are no longer at all: for they cannot be completed except by passing away. He says, therefore: Heaven and earth will pass away. As if to say: Everything with you that is lasting and without change is not lasting unto eternity, and everything that is seen to pass with me is held fixed and without passing, because my speech, which passes, expresses abiding judgments. But my words will not pass away. And since my words are so undoubtedly to be fulfilled, see that you not, against the testimony of my words, give yourselves to surfeiting and drunkenness and worldly cares, as some will in the time of the imminent judgment: of whom it is said: When they say, Peace and security, sudden destruction will come upon them (1 Thess. 5).
21.37: 21.37 And he was, etc. What he taught in word he confirms by example. He who warned, in view of the universal judgment and the uncertain end of individuals, to renounce the pleasures and cares of the age, and to watch and pray, himself, with his passion imminent, persists in teaching, vigils, and prayers, and rouses by word those for whom he was to suffer, and commends them in prayer to the Father. So we too, when we live justly and piously amid prosperity, should not despair of divine mercy amid adversity. By day we teach in the temple, because we give the faithful the form of good work; by night we stay on the Mount of Olives, because in the darkness of straits we breathe again in the consolation of spiritual joy.
22.1: 22.1 Was drawing near, etc. Which is called the Passover, etc. Pascha is named not from passion but from passing over, because on that day the destroyer passed over Egypt, or the Lord, freeing his people; by which name was signified that the Lamb on this day would pass from the world to the Father. Between Passover and unleavened bread there is this difference: Passover is the name of the single day on which the lamb was slain in the evening, that is, the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month. The days of unleavened bread were from the fifteenth day of the moon to the twenty-first day of the same month. But the evangelists use them indifferently, the day of unleavened bread for Passover, and Passover for the days of unleavened bread; hence Luke here: The feast day of unleavened bread, which is called Passover (Luke 12), because the day of Passover was also commanded to be celebrated with unleavened bread. And we, making as it were a perpetual Passover, are commanded always to pass from this world: on one day the lamb is sacrificed in the evening, and seven days of unleavened bread follow, because Christ, having suffered once for us in the fullness of times, commanded that during the whole time of the age (which is passed in seven days) we should live in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
22.2: 22.2 And they sought, etc. Matthew testifies that this was done two days before the Passover, when the chief priests and scribes were gathered in the court of Caiaphas.
22.3: 22.3 Entered. John says that after the morsel handed over by the Lord, Satan entered into Judas. But Satan had also possessed him before the morsel, and he whom he had earlier entered to deceive, he entered afterward to possess more fully, now handed over to him.
22.7: 22.7 Then came the day. Although he was crucified on the following day, that is, on the fifteenth day of the moon, yet on this night in which the Lamb was sacrificed he also handed over to his disciples the sacraments of his flesh and blood to be celebrated, and, seized and bound by the Jews, he consecrated the beginning of that sacrifice itself, that is, of his passion.
22.10: 22.10 Behold, entering. As God foreknowing all things, he speaks with the disciples of things that are done elsewhere. And fittingly a man carrying a jar of water meets those about to prepare the Passover, to show that the mystery of this Passover is to be celebrated for the washing of the world through the water of baptism, where for worshipers of the true Passover the typical fervor is removed from the threshold, and the baptism of the life-giving fountain is consecrated for the taking away of sins. The jar signifies the perfect measure of the fulfilled time in which it was fitting for these things to be done. A man with a jar. He is designated without a name, so that he be thought poor and of no note, he who is chosen by the Lord. His holiness appears in this, that the Lord with his disciples rests in his guest-chamber with the delight of lofty virtues. Follow. The names, whether of the water-bearer or of the Lord of the house, are purposely omitted, so that opportunity be signified as to be given to all who wish to be steeped in the sacraments of Christ (which is to celebrate the Passover) and to those seeking to receive Christ into the lodging of their mind.
22.12: 22.12 A large upper room. The law is spiritual, which, going out of the straits of earth, receives the Savior in a lofty place. He who remains in the letter makes the Passover in lowly places, but he who follows the water-bearer, that is, the herald of grace, into the house of the Church, passing beyond the surface of the letter, prepares refreshment for Christ on the throne of the mind, when he understands that all the sacraments of the Passover, and the other decrees of the law, were written of him.
22.15: 22.15 With desire I have desired, etc. He desires first to eat the typical Passover, and so to declare the mysteries of his passion to the world, that he may both prove the ancient Passover and demonstrate that this pertained to the figure of his dispensation, so that, truth now arriving, the shadow ought to cease. In figure of this the manna ceased, after the children of Israel ate of the fruits of the earth, and used that food no more.
22.16: 22.16 I will not eat. I will no longer celebrate the Mosaic Passover until what is the kingdom of God is fulfilled in the Church, spiritually understood. In this kingdom Christ eats even to this day, when what Moses commanded the rude people to observe carnally he exercises spiritually in his members.
22.17: 22.17 And having taken the cup. This cup belongs to the old Passover, which he was bringing to an end. Having taken it, he gives thanks, namely because the old things have passed and all things were to be new. He gave thanks. He shows what each should do under the scourge of his own fault, since he himself bore with equanimity the scourges of another's.
22.18: 22.18 For I say to you. As the typical eating of the lamb, so also the typical drinking of the Passover he says he will not drink until, the glory of the resurrection shown, the kingdom of God, that is, the faith of the world, comes, so that through the change of these two sacraments he may teach that the other sacraments or commands of the law are to be transferred to spiritual observance. It can however be taken simply: that from the hour of the supper until the time of the resurrection, when he was to come in the kingdom of God, he would not drink wine. For after the resurrection he ate and drank with the disciples.
22.19: 22.19 And having taken. The solemnities of the old Passover finished, he passes to the new, which in memory of his redemption he desires to be frequented in the Church, so that in place of the flesh and blood of the lamb he substitutes the sacrament of his own flesh and blood in the figure of bread and wine. He breaks and hands it, to show that the breaking of his body would not be without his own will. He gives thanks for the old things ended and the new things begun. With bread, etc. Because bread strengthens the body, wine produces blood.
22.21: 22.21 Nevertheless, etc. As he foretold the passion, so he foretold the betrayer, that seeing he cannot lie hidden, he may repent of the deed. Nor does he designate him by name, lest, openly corrected, he become more shameless. He therefore casts the fault into the number, that, conscious of it, he may do penance; he foretold also the punishment, that those whom shame had not convinced may be restrained by announced torments. The hand of him who betrays me. By the example of Judas he betrays the Son of man who presumes to violate that inviolable sacrament of the Lord's body. He sells who, neglecting fear and love of him, is convicted of loving perishable and criminal things.
22.24: 22.24 There arose, etc. BEDE. The cause of the contention is unknown to us, but it is not incredible, etc., up to let us see what the spiritual teacher commanded. AMBROSE. Let us therefore be on our guard with all care, etc., up to that it be not a boast about precedence but a contention about humility.
22.25: 22.25 But he said to them. The kind teacher does not accuse them of the contention begun, but describes the form of humility which they should follow; as if to say: You, in the manner of worldly people, wish to come to possession of the kingdom through preferment, but one comes to the summit of the virtues not by power but by humility. It is necessary that the subject find correction a mother in piety and a father in discipline, lest strictness be harsh or piety be lax.
22.27: 22.27 For who, etc. To fulfill the words of exhortation he sets forth an example from himself. Hence John writes (John 13): If I, the Lord and Master, have washed your feet, etc. In the word ministering can be included everything the Lord did in the flesh, not only by preaching or applying miracles, but also by laying down the soul which he took for us, that we too may learn to lay down our souls for one another.
22.28: 22.28 You have continued with me. My weakness did not disturb you, but you persevered in the good begun. As, therefore, to me persevering unto death the Father gave the name which is above every name (Phil. 3), so I too will lead you who persevere with me to the eternal kingdom. It is to be understood that Judas had already left, and many others had already gone back, having heard the words of the incomprehensible sacrament when the Lord was speaking these things.
22.30: 22.30 And sit upon thrones. This is the change of the right hand of the Most High, that those who now humbly rejoice to serve their fellow servants may then, exalted, be fed at the Lord's table with perpetual feasts, and those who, unjustly judged in temptations, remain with the Lord may there come with him as just judges over their tempters. For the more despised they are here, the greater the height of power they will grow to there. Judging the twelve. By twelve is signified not twelve persons but a multitude of judges, on account of the two parts of the number seven, by which totality is signified, that is, three and four, by which twelve is multiplied.
22.31: 22.31 And the Lord said. Lest the twelve glory that they alone out of so many thousands were said to have remained with the Lord in his temptations, he warns them that they could have been crushed by the same storm had they not been protected by divine grace. And when Satan demands to tempt, and to shake as one who cleans wheat by winnowing, we are taught that no one is tempted by the devil unless God permits. Behold Satan, etc. Satan asks for the good to be sifted when he pants with the heat of malice for their affliction. The more he envies and desires their temptation, the more he, as it were, asks for their testing, though he begs for something else.
22.32: 22.32 But I have prayed. Not that you not be tempted, but that your faith not fail, that after the fall of denial you may rise again by repenting to your former state. For it is useful for the saints also to be tested by temptations, that either when tempted it may appear how strong they were, or, having known their weakness through temptation, they may learn to become stronger, and so when they have been proved they may receive the crown of life.
22.33: 22.33 Who said to him, etc. Because the Lord had said he prayed for Peter, he, conscious of his present affection and fervent faith but ignorant of the future fall, does not believe he could fail from him. But he who knows what is in man, lest anyone incautiously trust in his standing or more incautiously distrust because of a fall, as God foretells the manner, time, and number of his denial, and as the merciful one promises the help of his defense.
22.35: 22.35 When I sent you. He does not instruct the disciples by the same rule of living in time of persecution as in peace. For when the disciples were sent to preach, he commanded them to take nothing for the way, ordaining that he who announces the Gospel should live by the Gospel. But with the crisis of death at hand, and that whole nation persecuting shepherd and flock together, he decrees a rule suited to the time, permitting what is necessary for sustenance until, the madness of the persecutors subsided, the time of evangelizing returns.
22.36: 22.36 But now, etc. In this an example is given to us as well, that sometimes, when need presses, we can without fault relax something of the rigor of our purpose. For example: if we travel through inhospitable regions, it is allowed to carry more for the journey than we have at home. And he who has not. He commands either to take a sword or a garment, or not a garment to buy, so that readers may know that the disciples did not lack the ability to resist, but rather had love for the teacher in suffering, where, even if there were no other reason for drawing the sword, this could suffice, that, the servant's ear being cut off, it was healed by the Lord's touch. In this we are admonished not to endure the anger of the one struck, but to receive the faith of those rising again.
22.38: 22.38 Behold, two swords. Two swords are produced, one of the New and the other of the Old Testament, by which we are fortified against the devil's snares. And he says: It is enough. Two swords suffice for the testimony of the Savior who suffered willingly. One, which would teach the apostles the boldness to fight for the Lord, and, the ear torn off by the sword's blow, that even in the Lord about to die there was piety and power to heal. The other, which, never drawn from its sheath, would show that they were not permitted to do all they could in his defense.
22.39: 22.39 And going out. The Lord, about to be betrayed by a disciple, goes to the accustomed place, where he could easily be found, lest he be thought to have feared death. And well he leads the disciples, steeped in the mysteries of his blood and body, to the Mount of Olives, to signify that all baptized in his death were to be strengthened by the most high gift of the Holy Spirit.
22.40: 22.40 Pray. It is impossible for man not to be tempted, and he does not say, that you not be tempted, but, that you not enter into temptation. Pray, that is, that temptation not overcome you and hold you within its nets.
22.41: 22.41 And he himself, etc. Having given the apostles the precept of praying, he too was withdrawn from them. He alone prays for all who alone was to suffer for all, indicating that his prayer, as much as his passion, is distant from ours. A stone's throw, etc. In this he mystically hints that they should direct the stone to the same point, that is, bring the intention of the law, which was written on stone, up to him; for that stone can reach up to him, since the end of the law is Christ for righteousness to everyone who believes (Rom. 10).
22.42: 22.42 Praying he said. He prays not so much from fear of suffering as from mercy for the former people, lest he drink from them the cup offered. Hence he significantly says: This, that is, of the Jewish people, who have no excuse of ignorance in my death, because daily I am announced to them in the law and the prophets. If therefore it can be that the multitude of the Gentiles believe without the destruction of the Jews, I refuse the passion. But if they are to be blinded so that others may see, not my will but yours be done. Father, if you will, etc. AMBROSE. He grieved for me when he had nothing for himself to grieve over. For he took up my sadness that he might bestow his joy on me. Confidently, then, I name sadness, I who preach the cross. Nevertheless, etc. The Lord, drawing near to the passion, took on himself the voice and fear of the weak in order to take them away; and again through obedience he showed fortitude of mind, so that when what we do not wish is impending, we may by weakness pray that it not happen, yet by fortitude be ready to fulfill the Maker's will rather than our own.
22.44: 22.44 And there came sweat. With death approaching, he expressed in himself the struggle of our mind, who rightly suffer a certain force of terror, since after a little while we are to find what will last forever. Of blood running down to the ground. By the earth moistened with blood it is declared that he was already obtaining the effect of his prayer, namely that he would cleanse with his blood the faith of the disciples which earthly frailty still convicted, and whatever scandal it had suffered at his death he would wipe out entirely by dying, and would raise the whole world dead in sins to life.
22.47: 22.47 To kiss him. The Lord receives the kiss, not to teach us to pretend, but that he might not seem to shun even the betrayer, and to affect the betrayer more, to whom he did not deny the offices of love. Hence it is said: With those who hated peace I was peaceable (Ps. 119).
22.49: 22.49 Lord, shall we strike with the sword? The order: When they had asked, saying: Lord, shall we strike with the sword? then he answered: Suffer thus far. That is, let not what is to come disturb you. They must be allowed to go thus far, to seize me, and that what is written of me may be fulfilled. But in the delay between the words of those asking and him answering, Peter, moved by greater eagerness to defend, struck for the Lord. But things which could be done at once could not be said at once. It is not therefore said, Suffer thus far, as though the Lord was pleased with Peter's deed, since in Matthew it is read that he said: Put your sword back in its place, which it appears Jesus said after the deed.
22.50: 22.50 The servant, etc. Mystically: The servant is the people of the Jews, unduly enslaved to the leaders, who in the Lord's passion lost the right ear, that is, spiritual understanding. The left remains, that is, content with the lowliness of the letter, the right being removed not by Peter taking it but by divine judgment laying it bare. This ear is restored by the Lord's mercy in those who preferred to believe.
22.52: 22.52 They had come to him, etc. According to the other evangelists, the chief priests and magistrates had not come to Jesus but had waited in the court of Caiaphas. But because they conducted the matter of the Lord's death so that they might seem as if innocent, since he was betrayed through a disciple, seized by a tribune and crowds, condemned by a governor, crucified by Romans, and Barabbas was chosen even by the people, the evangelist, wishing them to be the chief guilty ones by whose counsel everything was done, says they came to seize the Savior, who came by the power of their command. As against a thief, etc. It is foolish to seek with swords and clubs one who of his own accord offers himself to their hands, and by night to track down, through a betrayer, as if hiding and avoiding your eyes, one who teaches daily in the temple. But you gather against me in darkness, because your power, with which you arm yourselves against the light, is in darkness.
22.54: 22.54 Of the high priest. Of Caiaphas, who had bought the pontificate of one year for a price from the Roman emperor: first, however, to Annas, as John says: He followed from afar. Rightly from afar, he who was about to deny while near. It signifies the Church which will imitate the passion of Christ far differently, because the Church suffers for herself, Christ for the Church.
22.55: 22.55 A fire in the midst. A fire kindled at the instigation of the malignant spirit through desire armed the tongues of the faithless in the court of Caiaphas to deny and blaspheme God. For what the malignant council was doing within in the house of the high priest, the fire kindled outside amid the cold of night showed typically. Peter, numb for a time with this cold, wished to be warmed as it were by the coals of the servants, because he sought the solace of temporal comfort in the company of the faithless. But with the Lord looking on he left this unfaithfulness, and after the resurrection, at the catch of fish, when he saw coals laid and a fish on them, he inflamed his heart with the coals of love.
22.56: 22.56 A certain maid. Why does the maid betray him first, when men were more able to recognize him? Only to show that this sex had sinned in the death of the Lord, who was to redeem through the passion. And therefore a woman first received the mystery of the resurrection and kept the commands, to abolish the old error of transgression.
22.57: 22.57 But he denied. Not on the mountain, not in the temple, not in his own house does Peter deny, but in the praetorium of the Jews, in the house of the high priest, where there is no truth, where Christ was seized and bound. What but to go astray had he whom the doorkeeper of the Jews let in? Eve led Adam in badly; a woman brought Peter in badly.
22.59: 22.59 Man, I do not know what you are saying. He denies Christ not only who says he is not the Christ, but also who, though he is, denies that he is a Christian, and thus is fulfilled what the Lord says: You will deny me. He is a Galilean. The people of Jerusalem and the Galileans are equally Hebrews and of one language, but each province has its own peculiarities, and cannot change the native sound of speaking. And immediately. After the third denial follows the crowing of the cock. The sacraments of things are designated by the state of times. At midnight he denies, at cockcrow he repents. After the resurrection, at daybreak, he professed three times that he loved him whom he had denied three times, because he who had erred in the darkness of forgetfulness corrected it by the remembrance of the light now hoped for, and by the presence of the same true light fully raised up what he had supposed.
22.61: 22.61 And the Lord turning. By his look he provoked him to tears, as if recalling to his mind how often he had denied, as he had predicted to him; nor could he remain in darkness whom the light of the world looked upon.
22.62: 22.62 And going out. Shut out from the council of the impious, he washes away the fault, which was not permitted to linger within for this reason, that in the prince of the Church a remedy of penance might be established, and no one would dare trust in his own virtue.
22.63: 22.63 They mocked, etc. The prophecy was fulfilled: With a rod they shall strike the cheek of the judge of Israel. And likewise: I gave my cheek to blows. But he who was then beaten with the fists of the Jews is now beaten with the blasphemies of false Christians. They veiled his face, not that he might not see their crimes, but to hide from themselves (as they once did to Moses) the grace of knowing him: for if they believed Moses, they would believe the Lord also (John 8). This veil remains to this day over their hearts, but is taken away from believers: when he died the veil of the temple was torn.
22.64: 22.64 Prophesy. An insult to him who called himself a prophet. But heretics too, and Jews who to this day deny Christ, and bad Christians who provoke him with reprobate acts, while they think their thoughts and works of darkness are not seen by him, say as though mocking: Prophesy: who is it that struck you?
22.66: 22.66 If you are the Christ. They do not desire the truth, but prepare a slander. They understood that the Christ would be a mere man born of David. According to this, therefore, they ask, so that if he said, I am the Christ, they could slander him as arrogating royal power to himself.
22.67: 22.67 If I tell you. He had often said that he was the Christ. He had also asked them how they could say the Christ is the son of David when David calls him Lord, to provoke them by this to believe in God: but they were unwilling either to believe him when he spoke, or to answer when he asked, or to release him who was innocent.
22.69: 22.69 But from now on. Those who sought to slander the seed of David hear still more, that through contempt he will come to glory.
22.70: 22.70 You say. He tempers the answer so that he both speaks truth and the words do not lie open to slander. He preferred to prove himself the Christ, Son of God, rather than say it, that the ground for condemning might be taken away from those who confess what they allege.
22.71: 22.71 For we ourselves have heard. Where he said: The Son of man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God. They condemn themselves by their own judgment, who deliver to death one whom they recognize to be God by the testimony of his mouth and works.
23.1: 23.1 They led him. They handed him over to Roman power, so that in this way the Jews might show themselves to be strangers to his killing, in which not their innocence but their madness is shown.
23.3: 23.3 And Pilate, etc. Since two charges had been brought, namely that he forbade the paying of tribute and that he called himself Christ, Pilate could have heard what he had said about tribute: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and thence, thinking this a manifest lie of no account, he asked only what he did not know. You say it. With the same word by which he answers the chief priests, he answers the governor too, so that both are condemned by their own judgment.
23.4: 23.4 I find nothing. The day before the Lord suffered, he said to the disciples: The prince of this world comes, and he has nothing in me (Luke 20). But because the prince, that is Pilate, absolves him, in whom he found nothing deserving condemnation, see what the Jews do, who do not investigate the truth out of love of equity, but, goaded by envy, labor to condemn the just man.
23.5: 23.5 He stirs up the people. They accuse not him but themselves. For to have taught the people, and by teaching to have roused them from their former sluggishness of body, and by such action to have passed from Galilee to Judea, that is, through the whole land of promise, from end to end, is not a charge of crime but a judgment of virtue. Finally Pilate, thinking the Savior not to be questioned about this, but rather having found an occasion, desires to return him free of judgment by him.
23.7: 23.7 And when he learned. Lest he be forced to give sentence against an innocent man whom he knew had been handed over through envy, he sends him to Herod to be heard, so that he might be either absolved or condemned by his own tetrarch; but lest any excuse remain to the Jews, Herod too, who was a Jew by birth and religion, was permitted to show what he thought of Christ, so that both regions, Judea where Christ was born and Galilee where he was raised, might be shown to have conspired in his death. But he answered him nothing. He was silent and did nothing, both because Herod's unbelief did not deserve to see divine things and because the Lord avoided display. In Herod all the impious are signified, who do not believe the law and the prophets and cannot see the works of Christ in the Gospel. While the chief priests accused him, he answers little before Pilate and nothing before Herod, lest by clearing himself of the charge and being released by the prince he put off the usefulness of the cross.
23.11: 23.11 And he mocked him. That he is scorned and mocked in a white garment signifies that the lamb was sacrificed in chaste flesh for the sins of the whole world, suffered and was buried: that here he is mocked clothed in a white garment, whereas according to the other evangelists in a purple or scarlet one, signifies the twofold kind of martyrdom with which the Church is adorned in her sufferings, so as to be white in action and ruddy in blood. For she herself, flourishing with the little flowers of her members, brings forth lilies in peace and roses in war. And sent him back to Pilate. He is sent to Herod, sent back to Pilate, and though neither pronounces him guilty, yet each yields to the goads of another's iniquity.
23.12: 23.12 And they became friends. The unspeakable pact which Herod and Pilate made in killing Christ, their successors keep by hereditary right, since Jews and Gentiles, divided in race and religion as in mind, yet agree in persecuting Christians and destroying the faith of Christ. In the type of Herod and Pilate, who became friends through Jesus, the figure of the Jews and Gentiles is preserved, so that through the passion of Christ the concord of both peoples was to come about, yet in such a way that the Gentile first takes the kingdom of God and transmits the devotion of his faith to the Jew, so that they too may clothe with the glory of his majesty the body of Christ, whom they had earlier despised.
23.14: 23.14 You brought. Note how much zeal Pilate has to release Jesus. First, while they accuse, he says he found no cause in him; then, as they persist in what they had begun, he sends him to Herod to find out whether he could find any crime in him or decide he should be released. Finally, Herod's will having been learned and no wrongdoing found in Jesus, he seeks the people's judgment, to whom one must be released at the Passover. Again, a third time, wishing to release him, he asks. But the more earnestly he seeks to release, the more criminal he finds them in his death.
23.15: 23.15 But neither Herod. To reproach the hardness of the Jews or Gentiles, Pilate admits that neither he nor Herod found anything in killing and mocking Christ, but obeyed the clamor of another's cruelty.
23.16: 23.16 Having chastised him, therefore, etc. Pilate absolves Jesus whom he shows to be innocent, but that the Scriptures might be fulfilled, he absolves him by judgment, yet crucifies him by mystery.
23.18: 23.18 Away with this man, etc. Because they chose a robber instead of Jesus, a murderer instead of the Savior, a taker away instead of the giver of life, they rightly lost salvation and life, and submitted themselves so much to robberies and seditions that they lost both the country and kingdom they had preferred to Christ, and have not to this day recovered the liberty of soul or body which they had sold. Barabbas, etc. Barabbas, who is interpreted son of a teacher or of their father, is Antichrist himself, whom they will prefer to Christ, to whom it is said: You are of your father the devil. Pilate is interpreted mouth of the hammerer, and signifies the devil, who is the hammer of all matter, through whom God permits vessels to be tested, and finally crushes them when he breaks them in the last condemnation.
23.21: 23.21 Crucify, crucify him. Great cruelty: they seek not only to kill but to crucify, that, with hands and feet nailed to the wood, he might be put to death by prolonged dying, so that the pain would not end too soon, and that he might be seen long on the cross.
23.22: 23.22 I will chastise, etc. This chastisement he gave, by mocking and scourging, to the desires of the wicked, that they might not rage up to crucifying. This both the words of John the evangelist and the very pillar to which the Lord was bound attest, which to this day shows to those who look sure signs of the Lord's blood. But though Pilate does this, the insatiable fury of the sacrilegious does not cease, but presses on more, because they saw the accusation they had brought against the Lord emptied by Pilate's careful questioning. At last the shameless turn only to entreaties, so that what they could not do by accusing or, as it were, reasoning, they now accomplish by demanding and clamoring and completing.
23.25: 23.25 And he released, etc. The author of sedition and murders is released to the Jews, that is, the devil, who for his fault was driven from the fatherland of light and sent into the prison of darkness, and therefore they cannot have peace, because they did not choose the author of peace.
23.26: 23.26 They seized one, etc. At first the Lord carried the cross, but afterward it was laid on Simon, whom they met as they went out, and this fittingly: for Christ suffered for us, that you should follow in his steps (1 Pet. 2). But whoever wishes to follow him, let him take up his cross and follow. Because Simon was not an Israelite but a Cyrenian, the Gentiles are designated by him, formerly strangers and guests of the covenants, but now in faith citizens and members of God's household and co-heirs of Christ; hence Simon is interpreted obedient heir of Cyrene. But Simon comes from the country, that is, from the village, whence pagans, who being alien to the city of God are ignorant of urban conduct. But Simon, leaving the village, carries the cross after Jesus, when the peoples of the Gentiles, having abandoned pagan rites, obediently embrace the footsteps of the Lord's passion.
23.27: 23.27 There followed, etc. But not with the same mind do they follow the cross: the wicked follow to look gladly on one dying. The women, to weep for him whom they desired to live, as about to die, dying, and dead. The lament of the women alone is mentioned not because many men did not also grieve, but because the female sex, being as it were more contemptible, could more freely show, in the presence of the chief priests, what it felt against them. But because the Lord knows who are his (2 Tim. 2), passing over the crowd of the raging people, he turns his eyes and lips to the women who love and lament him. Who lamented. They grieved over the mortal life which was to be ended by death, not over the blind who were killing the physician.
23.28: 23.28 Daughters of Jerusalem. Note that when he calls them daughters of Jerusalem, not only those who had come with him from Galilee, but many women who were citizens of the same city had also attached themselves to him. Do not weep. Do not lament me as about to die, whose resurrection can quickly undo death, whose death will destroy death and the author of death himself. Rather wash yourselves and your offspring with worthy fountains of tears, lest you be condemned with the faithless in vengeance for my cross.
23.29: 23.29 Behold, the days are coming. The days of the Roman siege and captivity. It is natural, when captivity is imminent and hostile slaughter is raging through fields and cities, for all who can escape to seek every high or hidden refuge in which to hide.
23.30: 23.30 Fall upon us. This can be understood, beyond what is needed, of those who of either sex made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven.
23.31: 23.31 For if in the green wood. The green wood is Christ and his elect, the dry the impious and sinners, whence he says: If I, then, who have not sinned, who am rightly called the tree of life and bear twelve fruits of grace in each month, do not depart from this world without the fire of the passion, what torments await those who are empty of fruits, and moreover do not fear to give the tree of life to the flames? And if now is the time for judgment to begin at the house of God, and all who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecution, what will be the end of those who do not believe the Gospel? (1 Pet. 4; 1 Tim. 3).
23.32: 23.32 And there were led. What was said is fulfilled: And he was reckoned with the wicked (Isa. 53). In death he is reckoned with the wicked, that in the resurrection he may give life to the wicked, he who became man for men gave men the power to become children of God.
23.33: 23.33 The place of Calvary. Outside the gate of Jerusalem were places where the heads of the condemned were cut off, and they were called places of Calvary, that is, of the beheaded. There he is crucified, so that where the place of the condemned was, the banners of martyrdom might be raised. And robbers, etc. The Jews' iniquity in the deed is execrable, which crucifies as a robber the Redeemer of all; yet the robber is good in the mystery, who lay in wait for the devil to carry off his vessels. By the one on the right is signified the mortification of the flesh for heavenly glory; by the one on the left, the mortification of the flesh for some worldly cause.
23.34: 23.34 And Jesus, etc. Because Luke undertook to write of Christ's priesthood, the Lord rightly intercedes with God for his persecutors by the right of a priest, and opens paradise to the confessing robber, nor does he pray in vain, but obtains it for those who believed after his passion. He does not pray for those who through envy and pride understood the Son of God, deny and crucify him, but for those who, having zeal for God but not according to knowledge, did not know what they did. Dividing. John speaks of this more fully. The garment in four parts signifies the Church spread through the whole world, which consists of four parts, distributed equally to all parts, that is, concordantly. The tunic, cast lots for, signifies the unity of all parts, which is held by the bond of charity. Lots. In the lot the grace of God is commended. For so it comes in one to all, when the lot pleased all, because the grace of God too comes in unity to all, and when a lot is cast, it is trusted not to anyone's person or merits but to the hidden judgment of God.
23.35: 23.35 He saved others. They condemn themselves by their own judgment, who even unwillingly confess that he saved others. He could indeed have saved himself, but being himself the Christ, the chosen of God, he did not wish to come down from the cross. For he who came to be crucified for us neglected to save himself from the cross because, along with the other sinners, he took care by dying to save even the crucifiers.
23.36: 23.36 And they mocked him, etc. Note that the Jews mock the title of Christ and Son of God, handed down to them by the authority of Scripture. But the soldiers, ignorant of the Scriptures, insult not Christ the chosen of God but the king of the Jews. And offering vinegar. The Jews were vinegar, degenerating from the wine of the patriarchs. With this vinegar the soldiers give the Lord to drink, whom at their suggestion they hand over to death.
23.38: 23.38 And there was, etc. These three languages stood out above the rest. Hebrew, on account of the Jews who gloried in the law; Greek, for the wisdom of the Gentiles; Latin, for the Romans who ruled. Therefore, whether the Jews like it or not, every kingdom of the world, all worldly wisdom, all the sacraments of the divine law testify that Jesus is the emperor of those who believe and confess. This is the king of the Jews. The title which testifies that Christ is king is placed not below but above the cross, because although on the cross he suffered in human weakness, yet above the cross he shone with the majesty of a king, and therefore the title is placed above the one sacrificed, so that it may be plain to all who wish to read, that is, to believe, that through the cross he did not lose but strengthened his dominion.
23.40: 23.40 Rebuked him. The very rebuke reveals the future scandal of the cross even among believers, some on the right, some on the left.
23.42: 23.42 Lord, remember me. Great grace stands out in this robber. He has no member free from torment except heart and tongue, and all he has free he offers. With the heart he believes, with the mouth he confesses. He had faith who believed that he would reign whom he saw dying with himself. He had hope who asked for entrance. He held charity firmly who both rebuked the other robber for his iniquity and preached to him the life he had come to know. Great is the virtue: he confesses him whom he sees dying in human weakness, whom the apostles denied, whom they had seen doing miracles by divine power.
23.43: 23.43 Amen I say to you. A most beautiful example for aiming at conversion, that pardon is so quickly granted to the robber, and richer grace than the prayer. For the Lord always gives more than is asked: he asked, Remember me, etc.; the Lord says: Today you will be with me, etc. The Lord forgives quickly, because he is quickly converted.
23.44: 23.44 And darkness, etc. The sun drew in its rays so as not to see the Lord hanging, or lest the impious blasphemers enjoy its light. And note that at the sixth hour, that is, when the sun is about to leave the center of the world, he is crucified; at dawn, that is, at sunrise, he rises, because he died for our sins and rose for our justification (Rom. 18). When Adam sinned after midday, that is, when the light of faith had declined, the voice of the Lord was heard; at the same moment of time in which paradise had been closed to Adam when he then sinned, now the Lord opens paradise to the penitent robber.
23.45: 23.45 The veil of the temple, etc. This happened as the Lord expired, but Luke anticipates, wishing to join the miracle of the sun to the miracle of the veil. The veil is torn so that the ark of the testament and all the sacraments of the law which were covered may appear and pass to the Gentiles. Josephus says that the angelic powers, once guardians of the temple, then likewise cried out together: Let us flee from these seats. Father, etc. Calling on the Father, he declares himself the Son of God. Commending his spirit, he implies not a failing of power but confidence in the same with a share of power. For he loves to give glory to the Father, in which he forms us to give glory to the Creator.
23.47: 23.47 And the centurion seeing. Seeing that he had power to send forth his spirit, which none has but the Maker of souls, he who had crucified him confesses, in the very scandal of the passion, the Son of God, whom the Jews after so many miracles refused to believe. Hence by the centurion the faith of the Church is designated, which, the veil of the heavenly mysteries opened through the Lord's death, soon affirms him just and Son of God while the Synagogue is silent.
23.48: 23.48 Striking their breasts. That they strike their breasts as a sign of penitence and mourning can be understood in two ways. Either they grieved that he whose life they had loved was unjustly killed; or they trembled that he whose death they remembered having obtained was more glorified in death. But whatever cause compelled them to beat the breast, let us see the difference between one people and another. The Gentiles, fearing God as the Lord dies, glorify him with the voice of open confession; the Jews, only striking their breasts, return home in silence.
23.50: 23.50 Named Joseph. Joseph, by the nobility of worldly power, is able to receive the body; by the justice of his merits he is worthy to bury it.
23.52: 23.52 He went, etc. Not the apostles, but Joseph, just and steadfast, and Nicodemus, in whom there was no guile, bury him. Such also is the burial of Christ, which has no fraud or iniquity, by which the evasion of the Jews is blocked. For if the apostles had buried him, they would say that he whom they said was stolen was not buried.
23.53: 23.53 In a linen cloth. From the simple burial of the Lord the ambition of the rich is condemned, who cannot do without riches even when dead. Mystically: He wraps Jesus in a clean linen cloth who receives him with a pure mind. Hence the custom of the Church also is that the sacrifice of the altar be celebrated not on silk, not on dyed cloth, but on pure linen. And laid him. Well then is Christ laid in the tomb of a just man, that the Son of man may have where to lay his head, and rest in the dwelling of justice. Well in a new one, that he who receives Christ may walk in newness of life. He does not bury Christ unless he believes in Christ. In a tomb hewn out. The Lord alone is shut in a tomb, that his burial and resurrection may be shown to be unlike the frailty of our nature. He was buried, but as long as he willed; he rose, but when he willed. In which no one yet. If he were placed in a tomb where another had been placed, it would be pretended that another had risen. In a rock hewn out, lest, if it had been built of many stones, it be said that with the foundations of the tomb dug under he was taken away by theft.
23.54: 23.54 And it was the day, etc. On the sixth day man was made; on the sabbath God rested. On the sixth day, therefore, he is crucified and fulfills the mystery of the Preparation. Resting in the tomb on the sabbath, he awaits the event of the resurrection. So we in the sixth age of the world ought to suffer for the Lord. In the seventh, that is, when we die, the body is in the tomb, the soul with the Lord remains in rest after works, until in the eighth the bodies rise.
23.55: 23.55 The women. The other acquaintances of Jesus departing after the body was laid down, only the women, who loved more closely, watched the burial, to offer the gift of their devotion at a fitting time, waiting for what Jesus had promised, and therefore they saw first.
23.56: 23.56 And returning. Having seen the Lord's burial, they return and prepare spices and ointments: those who have read, heard, and remembered the Lord's passion turn to works of virtue in which Christ may delight, and keep silence on the sabbath. After the sabbath, about to come to the Lord with gifts, when the preparation of the present life is finished, they await rejoicing in blessed rest the time of the resurrection, in which they meet Christ with the fragrant spices of their actions. And on the sabbath, etc. The command was that the silence of the sabbath be kept from evening to evening. Therefore the women, the Lord having been buried, as long as it was lawful to work, are occupied in preparing ointments from the preparation day until sunset, and when the sabbath was past, at sunset, to come in the morning and anoint him, because on the evening of the sabbath, the moment of night already coming on, they could not approach the tomb.
24.1: 24.1 But on the first day of the week, etc. One of the sabbath is the same as the first of the sabbath, that is, one day from the day of the sabbath or sabbaths, which is now called Sunday. That the women came to the tomb very early shows the great fervor of charity in seeking and finding the Lord. Mystically: An example is given that, with faith enlightened and the darkness of vices shaken off, we should approach the sacred body of the Lord. For the sepulcher is a figure of the altar, on which the mystery of the body and blood of the Lord is celebrated. The spices which they bring signify the fragrance of virtues and the sweetness of prayers with which we ought to approach the altar.
24.2: 24.2 The stone rolled back. The rolling back of the stone signifies the unlocking of the sacraments of Christ, which were covered by the veil of the letter. The law was written on stone, and when its covering is taken away the Lord's body is not found dead but is proclaimed alive: because even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer (2 Cor. 5). He who came out from a closed womb could come out from a closed tomb.
24.4: 24.4 Perplexed in mind. They are perplexed in mind, because they were astonished that a stone of immense size had been rolled away, and grieved that so venerable a body was not found. As when the Lord was tempted in the wilderness, the victory completed, angels ministered to him, so now after death was conquered angels came, who announce the glory of the triumphant one not only by word but also by shining garb. And as they stood by the body in the sepulcher, so they daily attend the body consecrated on the altar.
24.5: 24.5 Bowed their faces. Note that neither the holy women are read to have fallen to the ground, nor any of the saints to have prostrated themselves on the ground in adoration at the Lord's resurrection; hence the custom began in the Church that in paschal time the knees are not bent in prayer, but one prays with the face bowed to the ground.
24.6: 24.6 Remember. On the third day, as we have from this passage, the Lord foretold that he would rise, among the disciples and also to the women who followed him. On the Preparation day at the ninth hour he expired; in the early morning of the first day of the week he rose. Rightly did he lie in the sepulcher one day and two nights, because he set the light of his single death (which was only in the flesh) against the darkness of our double death, which was in body and soul, and healed both of ours. For if he had taken on both, he would have freed us from neither.
24.8: 24.8 And they remembered. As the women standing at the Lord's tomb remember the words which he had spoken about his dispensation, so we, amid celebrating the mysteries of the Lord's passion, ought to remember not only the passion but also the resurrection.
24.9: 24.9 They told. As in the beginning the woman was the author of the fault to the man, and the man the executor of the error, so now she who had first tasted death saw the resurrection, and, lest she bear among men the reproach of perpetual guilt, she who had passed on the fault to the man passed on grace as well. And because the lower sex, weaker for carrying out, does not have the constancy of preaching, the office of evangelizing is committed to men.
24.11: 24.11 And they did not believe. That the disciples believed slowly was not so much their weakness as our future strength, for while they doubted, the resurrection is shown by many proofs, which, while we read and recognize them, what else are we but strengthened by their doubt?
24.12: 24.12 But Peter arising. John recalls that he and Peter ran together, and that when Peter entered the tomb and saw the linen cloths and the napkin, John himself, stooping down, saw the linen cloths and did not enter. But it is to be understood that Peter first, stooping down, saw what Luke recalls, which John passes over: later, however, he entered to discern the inner things more carefully, but entered before John entered.
24.13: 24.13 Named Emmaus. Emmaus is itself a metropolis, a notable city of Palestine, which after the conquest of Judea was restored under the emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, and with its condition changed its name as well.
24.15: 24.15 While they were talking. As they speak about him, the Lord draws near and accompanies them, both to kindle in their minds the faith of the resurrection and to fulfill what he had promised: Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them (Matt. 28). Drawing near, etc. Eyes, etc. He appeared indeed in his own form, but did not show the form they would recognize. As they both loved him within and yet doubted, so he outwardly present is there and does not show who he is. To those speaking of him he shows his presence, but from those doubting of him he takes away the form of recognition.
24.18: 24.18 Are you a stranger, etc. To whom, etc. They think a stranger the one they do not recognize. And truly he was a stranger to them, from whose frailty he stood far off by the glory of the resurrection, and from whose faith, ignorant of the resurrection, he remained estranged. A man, a prophet, etc. And how they handed him over, etc. They confess a prophet and a great one, but are silent about the Son of God, either because they do not yet believe perfectly, or, if they believe, fear to be handed over into the hands of the Jews, not knowing with whom they are speaking.
24.21: 24.21 But we, etc. In a way they rebuke themselves, because they had hoped for redemption in him whom they had seen dead and did not believe would rise, and they grieve most that he was killed without fault, whom they knew to be innocent, and on this account they walked sad.
24.22: 24.22 They frightened us, etc. Rightly they are said to have frightened those to whom, about the body not being found, they added more sadness than the joy they brought from the announced resurrection to cheer them.
24.24: 24.24 Some went, etc. Since above he said that Peter ran to the tomb, and now Cleopas says: Some of ours went to the tomb, etc., it is to be understood that two went together. But he first mentions Peter alone, because Mary first told him.
24.25: 24.25 O foolish and slow of heart. Here a twofold necessity of humbling lies upon us, who are neither taught in the Scriptures as much as we should, nor intent on fulfilling what we know as much as is fitting. For if Moses and the prophets spoke of Christ, and foretold that he would enter into glory through the passion, how does he glory in being a Christian who neither investigates in the Scriptures how they pertain to Christ, nor desires to reach through sufferings the glory he wishes to have with Christ?
24.28: 24.28 And he, etc. Stay with us, etc. He showed himself in body such as he was in their mind. They had to be tested, whether they would love as a stranger him whom they did not yet love as God. But because those with whom the truth walked cannot be strangers to its brightness, they call him to lodging, indeed compel him. From this example it is gathered that strangers are to be not only invited to lodging but even drawn.
24.30: 24.30 He broke, etc. Him whom they did not recognize in the exposition of Scripture they recognized in the breaking of bread, because not the hearers of the law but the doers will be justified, and the truth is understood better by doing than by hearing.
24.31: 24.31 Were opened, etc. The appearance of weakness is withdrawn from carnal eyes, that the glory of the resurrection may begin to appear to their minds.
24.32: 24.32 And they said, etc. Mystically: Therefore another form was shown to them in Christ, that they might not recognize him except in the breaking of bread, so that all may understand that they do not acknowledge Christ unless they become sharers of his body, that is, of the Church, whose unity the Apostle commends in the sacrament of bread, saying: We, though many, are one bread, one body (1 Cor. 10). When therefore he hands over the blessed bread, their eyes are opened to recognize him, and the impediment that was in their eyes from Satan, lest Jesus be recognized, is removed. And the Lord permits this impediment to remain until the sacrament of bread is reached. But when the unity of the body is shared, the impediment of the enemy is taken away so that Christ can be recognized. Burning. GREGORY. The word having been heard, the heart, earlier cold from the torpor of unbelief and fear, is kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit, so that it now burns with heavenly desire and stretches itself to believe the truth. As many precepts as instruct a man, so many torches inflame him.
24.34: 24.34 The Lord is risen. The report that Jesus had risen, made by those women and by Simon Peter to whom he had appeared, these two had found them speaking; but they themselves had also heard before that he had risen, but they feared to say it on the road when they said only that angels had been seen by the women. For, not knowing him with whom they were speaking, they could fear falling into the hands of the Jews if they said anything openly about the resurrection of Christ.
24.36: 24.36 Jesus stood, etc. This appearance is the one of which John says (John 20): When it was evening on that day, etc., and he said to them: Peace be with you. As to what John says, that Thomas was not with them, while Luke says these two found the eleven gathered, and those who were with them, it is to be understood that Thomas had gone out from there before the Lord appeared to them as they were speaking this.
24.37: 24.37 To see a spirit. And he said to them. The disciples knew he had been a true man, but after he died they do not believe that on the third day true flesh could rise from the tomb. They think, therefore, that they see the spirit which he gave up in the passion, but the Lord takes away this error. Why are you troubled. AMBROSE. The apostles believed, and yet are troubled, etc., up to that the Lord, the doors being closed, suddenly poured himself in with his body. Thoughts, etc. False ones, not descending from above, but like a bad weed rising in the heart; I demand the faith I planted in you, I condemn what has sprung from you; if there is no truth in the resurrection, the fruit of the passion is lost.
12.56: 12.56 Hypocrites, etc. And lest some unlearned people in the crowd, flattering themselves about their ignorance, excuse themselves by saying that they do not know the law and the prophets, he assumes that they can discern by natural reason either that he who does works which no one else had done is above man and is God, or that after so many injustices of the age the just judgment of the Creator is to come.
12.58: 12.58 And when you go. When in this life you prepare yourself to see the placated face of the judge, although the word of God is contrary to your flesh, yet use it as a guard given to you on this journey, lest it, despised, accuse you. With your adversary. Our adversary on the way is the word of God, contrary to our carnal desires in the present life; he is freed from it who is humbly subject to its commands. Otherwise the sinner, guilty through contempt of the word, will be held in the judge's examination, and the judge will hand him over to the exactor, that is, the devil; for he will permit the devil to drag his soul to punishment, and the exactor himself, who demands the penalty for the guilt he suggested, will thrust it back into hell. Give diligence, etc. These words also pertain to trampling on the enticements of the world and awaiting the judge's coming. As if to say: Since it is certain that a strict judge is coming, so live here that you may not be condemned in that judgment.
12.59: 12.59 You pay. He always pays the penalties for his sins by suffering, but never obtains pardon.
13.1: 13.1 Now there were present. While the teacher of truth was instructing those present how they ought to prepare themselves for the judge's coming and how those who do not prepare are to be condemned, he is told about the Galileans, as though they had justly suffered because they had not prepared themselves well; and the Lord answers that they were truly sinners and justly perished, and that other sinners will likewise perish if they do not recognize themselves as sinners. Telling him. As if they said: It appears that these were sinners and to be condemned forever, who were killed by so wicked a death by an impious governor amid their sacrifices. About the Galileans. The Galileans paid the penalties of their crimes by a wicked death, yet it was not the death itself that harmed them so as to send them to the second death, but their evil life. They were punished, however, for the correction of the living, that when the pestilent man is scourged the fool may become wiser, or as an example for those unwilling to be corrected, and therefore for those who will perish most wretchedly.
13.3: 13.3 All, etc. This was fulfilled after the Lord's passion, when the Romans, beginning from Galilee, so devastated the unrepentant Jews that not only the courts of the temple but even the inner parts of the house, to which the Galileans had no access, were defiled with human blood.
13.4: 13.4 As those ten. These people of Jerusalem, like the Galileans, were not the only sinners but were punished to terrify the rest; those crushed by the fall of the tower signify the Jews who were unwilling to repent, who were to perish with their walls. Nor is it in vain that there are eighteen, a number which among the Greeks is expressed by iota and eta, that is, by the same letters with which the name Jesus begins. It signifies that the Jews will perish chiefly for this, that they were unwilling to receive the name of the Savior. That tower signifies him who is the tower of strength, which is rightly in Siloam, because Siloam, which is interpreted sent, signifies him who, sent by the Father, came into the world, who will crush all upon whom he falls.
13.6: 13.6 A fig tree. At the origin of the human race, Adam and Eve, when they had sinned, made girdles for themselves from the leaves of the fig tree. By the leaves of the fig tree, therefore, sins are understood. They were under the fig tree, as under the shadow of death, of whom it is said: For those who sat in the shadow of death a light has risen (Isa. 9).
13.7: 13.7 Seeking fruit. The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, in which house the Synagogue was planted like a fig tree in a vineyard. But he who allowed the sinner in the vineyard to be plundered by travelers also commanded this fig tree to be cut down. He seeks fruit in it, not as one who did not know whether it was there, but he shows in a figure that the Synagogue should already have had fruit. Nor does he seek before the time, who comes for three years. He who established the Synagogue through Moses, appearing in the flesh, himself teaches often in the Synagogue and seeks the fruit of faith, but does not find it in the Pharisees. And he said to the vinedresser. The vinedresser are the teachers and apostles, by whose prayers and warnings God's constant care is brought to mind, to whom the Lord often complains of the fruitless nation of the Jews, that during the three years of his visitation, that is, in the edicts of the law, the testimonies of the prophets, and the grace of the Gospel, it had been negligent. Why does it also use up the ground, etc. By the ground occupied by the barren fig tree the Jewish people can be signified, oppressed by the harmful shade of its leaders, so that it does not see the light of truth and is hindered by their examples from being warmed by the sun of love; hence Matt. 23: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, etc. He uses up the ground who does not exercise with good works the place he holds, who by the example of wickedness is a hindrance to others.
13.8: 13.8 Until I dig, etc. Until I strike fear into the humble root of the fruitless mind, both of present pressures and of eternal damnation. For a ditch is at the bottom, and rebuke, by showing the mind to itself, humbles it. He knows how to cultivate the ground who knows how to reprove vices. He understood that the hardness and pride of the Jews were the cause of barrenness. He promises therefore that hard hearts must be dug with apostolic mattocks, and the proud recalled to humility. I will put manure. That is, I will bring back to the mind the abomination of the evils it has done, and stir up the grace of compunction, with the fruits of good work, as it were from the richness of manure. For the sins of the flesh are called manure, which are applied to the root of the tree when the memory of thought of the wickedness of conscience is touched, and while one repents of it, as by the touch of manure, one returns to fruitfulness of work.
13.9: 13.9 And if indeed. Although the order of repentance required that he add, it will be spared, or something of the kind, he yet added nothing, but left the sentence suspended. But if not. Namely, if it does not bear fruit, he immediately attached the judgment of coming damnation, because he saw them more inclined to deny than to believe.
13.10: 13.10 Now he was teaching. The Lord is said to have taught this similitude of the fig tree in the Synagogue, to indicate that the parable belonged to the Synagogue itself. For that he seeks fruit in the fig tree and does not find it signifies that he lends his word to the Synagogue and it does not receive it; understanding, however, that it is not to be uprooted entirely but that a remnant is to be saved through faith, there follows immediately in the same place the healing of the primitive Church under the appearance of the bent woman. For the fig tree preserved signifies the same as the woman made upright. On the sabbaths. On the sabbaths he teaches and raises the bent woman, because through the word of preaching he leads those raised from temporal to eternal things to the rest of the resurrection.
13.11: 13.11 Behold a woman, etc. This woman could be raised up only after eighteen years, because human nature will not be able to lay aside this corruption and be raised to put on the incorruption of eternal blessedness unless it first fulfills the law contained in the ten commandments, and the grace in which the resurrection of Christ has been accomplished and ours is awaited. Years, etc. The number six, in which the creation of the world was completed, signifies the perfection of works; multiplied by three it gives eighteen, and signifies those who in the three times of the Lord's visitation, namely before the law, under the law, and under grace, have perfection of works. In this time, then, Judea was bent from the uprightness of her mind, she who knew earthly things more than heavenly, and works.
13.14: 13.14 Because on the sabbath. God rested on the sabbath from the works of the world. Hence Moses also commanded that on the sabbath one keep holiday from servile and harmful action, prefiguring the time when our worldly works, but not religious ones, that is, the praising of God, will cease. As a sign of this the Lord also heals on the sabbath. But the ruler of the synagogue, not understanding this, is deceived and deceives, because the law forbade on the sabbath not to heal a man but to do servile works, that is, to be burdened with sins.
13.15: 13.15 Hypocrites. Rightly he calls them hypocrites, that is, pretenders, who, while they desire to be seen as teachers of the people, are not ashamed to put the healing of a man after the care of livestock. Does not loose his ox. Mystically: The ox that knows its owner and the ass that knows its master's crib signify the Jewish and the Gentile people, each of which, released from the bonds of sin, has laid aside the thirst and heat of this world by drinking from the Lord's fountain. In these two animals, therefore, the Lord foretells the calling of the two peoples, the Jews opposing.
24.39: 24.39 Feel and see. He persuades of the resurrection by many proofs, offering himself both to be seen with the eyes and handled with the hands, and while he shows by touching the bones and flesh, he signifies the state of his own or our resurrection, in which our body will be both subtle through the effect of spiritual power and palpable through the truth of nature. After the resurrection the Lord showed in his body two contrary things: the palpable, of the same nature, to form us in faith, and the incorruptible, of another glory, to invite us to the reward.
24.40: 24.40 He showed them his hands, etc. So that by showing the scars of the wounds he might heal the wound of unbelief; scars which he kept then, and will keep in the judgment. First, to build up faith in the resurrection; then, that, interceding with the Father for us, he may always show what kind of death he bore for man; third, that to those redeemed by his death he may make known, by the exhibited signs of that same death, how mercifully they have been helped. But last, that in the judgment he may declare how justly the impious are condemned, by showing the scar he received from them. He did not keep the scars, therefore, from inability to heal them, but to bear about a perpetual triumph of his victory.
24.41: 24.41 Have you anything here. To make known the truth of the resurrection, he wished not only to be touched but to eat with them, not that he or we after the resurrection should need food, but to show that he was a body and not a spirit; he ate by power, not by necessity. The thirsty earth absorbs water in one way, the burning ray of the sun in another: the one by need, the other by power.
24.42: 24.42 Of broiled fish. The broiled fish is the mediator himself who suffered, caught in the waters of the human race by the snare of death, broiled at the time of the passion. He too is the honeycomb for us in the resurrection. The honeycomb in the wax is the Godhead in the humanity. In the eating of this honey it is signified that he receives into his body to eternal rest those who, when they feel tribulations for God, do not depart from the love of inner sweetness. Those who are broiled here will there be satisfied with true sweetness.
24.43: 24.43 And when he had eaten. He removes all ambiguities: he was seen, touched, he ate, and lest he seem in anything to have mocked human senses, he sends them to the Scriptures, so that even if by magic arts he seems to have been able to do what he wished, as the pagans say, they may at least see that he could not have prophesied before he was born.
24.45: 24.45 Then he opened. After sight, after touch, after the law was recalled, he opened their understanding, that they might understand what they see and read; then, after commending the truth of his body, he commends the unity of the Church: And to be preached in his name.
24.46: 24.46 It behooved, etc. It was fitting that the ministers who were to preach repentance and remission to all nations should begin from Jerusalem. Not only because the oracles of God were entrusted to them, and theirs is the adoption of sons, and the glory, the covenants, and the giving of the law; but also so that the Gentiles, entangled in various errors and crimes, might be roused to the hope of pardon chiefly by this sign of divine piety, that he grants pardon to those who crucified the Son of God.
24.49: 24.49 But you, sit. After he had perfectly instructed the disciples about the power of preaching, though he could suddenly strengthen them if he wished, he delayed, saying: But you, sit. To give an example to those who follow, lest the imperfect presume to preach before the time. He sits in the city who confines himself within the cloisters of the mind, lest by speaking outwardly he wander, so that when he has been perfectly clothed with divine power, he may then go forth as it were from himself, instructing others.
24.50: 24.50 And he led them out. Passing over everything done during the forty days, he tacitly joins the last day, on which he ascended into heaven, to the first day of the resurrection. And fittingly, about to bless the disciples, he leads them out to Bethany, which is called house of obedience, because he who descended on account of the disobedience of the perverse ascended on account of the obedience of the converted.
24.53: 24.53 In the temple. So that in the place of prayer, amid the devotions of praises, they might await with hearts prepared in every way the promised coming of the Holy Spirit. So we, after celebrating in Jerusalem, that is, in the vision of peace, the solemnities of the passion and resurrection, with the Lord as leader let us seek Bethany, that with quiet mind we may be steeped in the sacraments of his body and blood, and take care to be a house of obedience. Praising and blessing. Luke, who undertook to set forth the priesthood of Christ more fully than the rest, and therefore began his Gospel from the ministry of the temple through the priesthood of Zechariah, beautifully completes it in the devotion of the temple, concluding there with the apostles, who are to be ministers of the new priesthood, not in the blood of victims but in the praise and blessing of God.
13.16: 13.16 And this woman, etc. A daughter of Abraham; every faithful soul is a daughter of Abraham, the Church gathered from both peoples to the faith, which, when the time of the law and of the Lord's resurrection was fulfilled, burst through the chains of long captivity by the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit: and so it is the same thing for an ox or ass to be loosed from the crib and led to drink, as for a daughter of Abraham to be raised up from the bond of harmful inclination.
13.17: 13.17 All were ashamed. Those who are ashamed at the Savior's words show themselves like the barren fig tree. Those who rejoice at the miracles, therefore, belong to the daughter of Abraham, that is, the Church, glorifying God for her being raised up. His adversaries. The scribes and Pharisees, who can neither openly contradict the truth nor, because of envy, are willing to believe. All the people rejoiced. The simple and humble, lovers of the words of truth and the miracles; and these are a figure of the Gentiles, who, while the Jews are blinded, are to be gathered to the faith through humility. Hence the Savior also commends their faith under the comparison of a grain of mustard seed.
13.18: 13.18 He said therefore. Since there were present those rejoicing and glorifying, he spoke for the commendation and instruction of those who are to be exalted in the Church through humility and fervor of faith.
13.19: 13.19 It is like, etc. The grain of mustard seed is a cheap and simple thing, but if it is crushed it pours out its strength. The kingdom of heaven, then, that is, the faith by which one comes to the kingdom, is compared to a grain of mustard seed: because at first it is humble and as if cast aside and of bitter taste on account of the weakness of Christ and the scandal of the cross; but ground down by adversities, it pours forth the grace of its power and fills those around with its fragrance, since it preached the glory of the resurrection and ascension even after death throughout the whole earth. Or the body of Christ is the grain of mustard seed, which Joseph took and buried in the garden, and which afterward grew in the resurrection and ascension. It spread out branches, sending preachers throughout the whole world, in whose sayings and consolations the faithful find respite from the weariness of the world.
13.21: 13.21 Which a woman took, etc. The woman is the Church, whose flour we are, as many as are ground by the exercise of fear and hope as by an upper and a lower millstone, that we many may be one bread in Christ. The Church therefore hides the leaven of love in three measures of flour, because she commands that we love God with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole strength.
13.22: 13.22 And he went, etc. He preached everywhere without distinction, not discriminating among persons, but seeking salvation for believers.
13.24: 13.24 Strive to enter, etc. As if he said: Truly few, and those with great labors, because unless the intention of the mind burns, the wave of the world, by which the soul is always called back to the depths, is not overcome.
13.25: 13.25 But when, etc. Christ the master of the house, although by his divinity he is everywhere, is said to be already inside with those whom, present in heaven, he gladdens by his vision, but is as if outside with those whom, struggling in this pilgrimage, he helps in secret. He will enter, then, when he leads the whole Church to the contemplation of himself. He will shut the door when he takes away from the reprobate the place of repentance; standing outside they will knock, that is, separated from the just, they will implore in vain the mercy they despised.
